questions.question: Batch processing is often contrasted with two other kinds of data system. Which three-way classification distinguishes systems by how work arrives and which performance measure matters most?

options.text: Online services, offline batch systems, and near-real-time stream processors
OLTP databases, OLAP data warehouses, and hybrid transactional-analytical systems
Synchronous, asynchronous, and partially synchronous models of distributed systems
Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless systems for replicating data

questions.explanation: Services wait for a client request and are judged mainly by response time (and availability). Batch systems run a job over a large, fixed input with no user waiting and are judged by throughput. Stream processors sit in between: like batch jobs they consume inputs and produce outputs rather than answering requests, but they act on events shortly after they occur, giving lower latency. The other groupings are real classifications, but of workload type, timing assumptions, or replication topology, not of how processing is triggered.

questions.question: Databases, caches, search indexes, and web servers typically share which style of interaction with their clients?

options.text: Request/response: a client sends a request or query and waits for the answer
Batch: a scheduled job processes a large fixed dataset and writes output files
Stream: events are consumed continuously shortly after they occur
Gossip: nodes periodically exchange state with randomly chosen peers

questions.explanation: These are online systems: a client asks for something or sends an instruction and, some time later, the system returns an answer while the client waits. Because someone is waiting, response time is the key metric. Batch and stream processing instead consume inputs and produce outputs without a per-request reply, and gossip is a protocol for nodes to spread state among themselves, not a client interaction style.

questions.question: In an online system such as a web server or an API service, what is generally assumed about an incoming request, and why does that make response time the key metric?

options.text: A human user triggered it and is waiting, so any delay is felt directly
Another machine triggered it and nobody waits, so only throughput matters
It is idempotent and can be retried freely, so latency hardly matters
It touches only one partition, so its latency is bounded by one node

questions.explanation: Online systems are built on the assumption that a request was triggered by a human user (a browser loading a page, or a service acting on a user's behalf) and that this user is waiting for the response. Long waits are visible to that person, so these systems pay close attention to response time. Idempotency and single-partition access are useful properties for some requests, but they are not what defines online processing.

questions.question: Which pairings of a kind of data system with its usual primary performance concern are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Online service: response time, with availability also very important
Batch processing system: throughput, i.e. how fast it crunches through a dataset of a given size
Stream processor: low latency from an event occurring to its effect on the output
All three: availability alone, since a reachable system is keeping up with its load

questions.explanation: A service has a waiting client, so response time dominates, and unavailability shows up as an error message to a user. A batch job has nobody waiting on each record; what matters is throughput, meaning how long it takes to process an input of a given size. A stream job processes events shortly after they happen, so its advantage over the equivalent batch job is lower latency. Availability matters for services, but being reachable says nothing about whether a batch job is fast or a stream processor keeps up.

optionExplanations.a: An online service handles one waiting client's request, so perceived response time and reachability dominate. High aggregate throughput does not compensate for a user-facing request that stalls.
optionExplanations.b: A batch job consumes a bounded dataset without a person awaiting each record, making total throughput the natural measure. The goal is to finish a given volume efficiently.
optionExplanations.c: A stream processor continuously turns newly arriving events into outputs, so event-to-result latency is central. Unlike batch processing, it does not wait for a bounded input to end.
optionExplanations.d: Availability only says requests can reach a system; it does not show that a batch job has good throughput or a stream is keeping up. Each processing style has a different primary performance concern.

questions.question: How long do batch jobs typically run, and how are they usually started?

options.text: Minutes to several days, usually started on a periodic schedule
A few seconds, each one started by an individual user request
Indefinitely, processing events as they arrive with no end point
Under a second, each one triggered by a write to the database

questions.explanation: A batch job takes a large amount of input data, processes it, and produces output; this can take from a few minutes to several days, so normally no user is waiting for it to finish. Batch jobs are therefore commonly scheduled to run periodically, for example once a day. Seconds-long work per user request is online processing, and jobs that never end because events keep arriving are stream processing.

questions.question: What property of the input most fundamentally separates batch processing from stream processing?

options.text: Whether the input is bounded (a fixed, finite dataset) or unbounded
Latency alone: batch is slow and stream is fast, with no structural difference
Whether the data is stored in a distributed filesystem or in a message queue
Whether the job is written in SQL or in a general-purpose programming language

questions.explanation: A batch job reads a bounded input, such as a fixed set of log files or a database snapshot, so it knows when it has read everything and eventually completes. A stream job's input is unbounded: more events may always arrive, so the job is never complete. Lower latency is a consequence of processing events soon after they occur, not the defining difference, and either style can use various storage systems and languages.

questions.question: When was the MapReduce paper published, and which open source systems implemented the model?

options.text: 2004; in Hadoop, CouchDB, and MongoDB, among others
1998; as the Google File System and as HDFS
2008; first in the Spark and Flink engines
2010; as the Pregel and Apache Giraph graph systems

questions.explanation: Google published MapReduce in 2004, and it was (perhaps overenthusiastically) called the algorithm that makes Google so massively scalable. The model was then implemented in open source systems including Hadoop, CouchDB, and MongoDB. GFS and HDFS are the distributed filesystems MapReduce runs on, Spark and Flink are later dataflow engines, and Pregel is a graph-processing model.

questions.question: Compared with the parallel processing systems built for data warehouses years earlier, what was MapReduce's main contribution?

options.text: A fairly low-level model, but a big step in the scale reachable on commodity hardware
A fundamentally new high-level programming model that made earlier parallel databases obsolete
A new declarative query language that replaced SQL for large-scale analytics
The first system ever to run parallel joins across a cluster of machines

questions.explanation: MapReduce was a lower-level programming model than the massively parallel (MPP) databases of the time, and the parallel processing and join algorithms it used had existed in those databases for over a decade. Its significance was the scale of processing it achieved on cheap commodity hardware. Although its importance has since declined, it is still worth understanding because it shows clearly why and how batch processing is useful.

questions.question: Which pre-computer technology is an early example of batch processing?

options.text: Hollerith punch-card tabulators, as used in the 1890 US Census
Jacquard looms, which read punched cards to control the pattern being woven
Telegraph networks that relayed individual messages station by station
Hand-cranked calculators that added one number at a time on demand

questions.explanation: Long before programmable digital computers, Hollerith punch-card tabulators computed aggregate statistics from large inputs for the 1890 US Census, a semi-mechanized form of batch processing. Electromechanical IBM card sorters used for business data processing in the 1940s and 1950s bear a strong resemblance to MapReduce's sort-then-aggregate pattern. Jacquard looms also read punched cards, but the cards controlled a machine rather than being data to aggregate; telegraphs and calculators handle one item at a time rather than processing a large input as a whole.

questions.question: A web server logs one line per request in nginx's default access-log format: remote address, remote user, local time, request, status, bytes sent, referrer, user agent. One line has these field values: 216.58.210.78; -; [27/Feb/2015:17:55:11 +0000]; GET /css/typography.css HTTP/1.1; 200; 3377; http://example.com/; Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/40.0.2214.115 ... Which conclusions are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That the request was made on February 27, 2015, at 17:55:11 UTC, for the file /css/typography.css, from the client IP address 216.58.210.78
That the user was not authenticated, so the remote_user field is set to a hyphen
That the response status was 200, meaning the request was successful, and the response was 3,377 bytes in size
That the browser was Chrome 40, and that the request carried no referrer header at all

questions.explanation: Each field is interpreted by its position in the declared log format. The line records a request at 17:55:11 UTC on 27 February 2015 from 216.58.210.78 for /css/typography.css; the hyphen in the remote-user field means the user was not authenticated; status 200 means success and 3377 is the response size in bytes. The browser was Chrome 40, but the referrer field contains a page URL, meaning the stylesheet was loaded because that page referenced it, so the claim that there was no referrer is false.

optionExplanations.a: The client address, UTC timestamp, request method, and path are explicit fields in the access-log format. They identify when, where, and from whom this request arrived.
optionExplanations.b: A hyphen in the configured remote-user field represents an unavailable authenticated username. It does not mean the client IP or all identity information is absent.
optionExplanations.c: HTTP status 200 records success, and the byte-count field records a 3,377-byte response body. Those positions must be interpreted using the server's declared log format.
optionExplanations.d: The user-agent does identify Chrome 40, but the referrer field holds a page URL, so a referrer was sent. Because the option denies that, the combined claim is false.

questions.question: A shell pipeline finds the five most requested URLs in an nginx access log, in which the requested path is the seventh whitespace-separated field. Its first stage after reading the file is awk '{print $7}'. What does that stage do?

options.text: It splits each line on whitespace and prints the seventh field
It prints the seventh line of the whole input file
It prints the seventh character of every input line
It keeps the first seven fields of each line and discards the rest

questions.explanation: awk splits each input line into fields on whitespace and, for {print $7}, outputs only the seventh field, which in this log format is the requested URL. The result is one URL per line, which later stages sort and count. In awk, $7 refers to a field within each line, not to the seventh line or the seventh character.

questions.question: In the pipeline cat access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -r -n | head -n 5, the first sort produces neither counts nor a ranking. Why is it needed?

options.text: It makes every repeated URL appear on adjacent lines, which uniq relies on
head requires its input to be sorted alphabetically before it can stop
awk emits fields in a random order that must be normalized first
It is redundant; uniq -c would give the same counts without it

questions.explanation: uniq only compares each line with the one immediately before it. Sorting the URLs first means that a URL requested n times appears as n consecutive lines, so uniq -c can count it while remembering only the current line. Without the sort, occurrences of one URL scattered through the input would be counted as many separate runs. MapReduce uses the same idea: the framework sorts mapper output by key so that all values for a key are adjacent when the reducer sees them.

questions.question: In the pipeline cat access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -r -n | head -n 5, what do uniq -c and the later sort -r -n do?

options.text: uniq -c collapses adjacent identical lines, prefixing each with its count; sort -r -n orders them by count, largest first
uniq -c removes duplicates anywhere in the input without counting them; sort -r -n sorts the URLs alphabetically in reverse
uniq -c counts the total number of lines in the input; sort -r -n sorts the URLs as if each URL were a number
uniq -c sorts the URLs and counts them in one step; sort -r -n simply reverses the order of the file's lines

questions.explanation: uniq filters out repeated lines by checking whether two adjacent lines are the same, and the -c option makes it output how many times each line occurred. Because it only looks at adjacent lines, it depends on the preceding sort. The second sort uses -n to compare the leading count numerically and -r to reverse the order, so the most requested URLs come first; head -n 5 then keeps the top five.

questions.question: A report of the five most requested URLs on a website shows these counts: 4189 /favicon.ico, 3631 for a blog article about SSH keys, 2124 for an article about schema evolution, 1369 for /, and 915 for /css/typography.css. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The top five URLs account for 12,228 requests in total
The single most-requested URL accounts for about 34% of that total
The top entry, /favicon.ico, is arguably not a 'page' at all — it is the browser's tab icon
The top five URLs between them account for about 8,000 requests

questions.explanation: The five counts sum to 12,228, and 4,189 divided by 12,228 is about 34.3%. The favicon entry is a browser-requested icon asset rather than a content page, so all three statements are true.

optionExplanations.a: Adding the five displayed request counts gives 12,228. This checks the aggregate directly rather than estimating from the visual ranking.
optionExplanations.b: Dividing the largest count, 4,189, by 12,228 yields about 0.343, or 34 percent. The percentage refers to the shown top-five total, not all server traffic.
optionExplanations.c: A favicon is an icon fetched by the browser for tabs or bookmarks, not normally a content page a person intentionally visits. URL counts can therefore need semantic interpretation.
optionExplanations.d: The displayed values already exceed 8,000 after only the first three rows, and their exact sum is 12,228. The smaller total results from ignoring part of the data.

questions.question: A Unix pipeline counts the most requested URLs in a web server log by extracting field 7 with awk, then sorting, counting with uniq -c, ranking, and taking the top five. You want to exclude CSS files, and separately to rank client IP addresses (field 1) instead of URLs. What needs to change?

options.text: Only the awk stage: add a condition excluding .css paths, or print $1 instead of $7
The whole pipeline must be rewritten from scratch for each of the two variations
The sort stage for the CSS filter, and the head stage for ranking client IP addresses
Neither can be expressed with awk, so a different toolchain is needed for both

questions.explanation: The later stages sort, count, and rank whatever single key per line awk emits. Excluding CSS needs only an awk condition such as '$7 !~ /\.css$/ {print $7}', and ranking client IPs needs only '{print $1}'. Changing one stage while the others stay the same shows how small single-purpose tools connected through a common text interface are easy to adapt.

questions.question: Which group consists of standard Unix text-processing tools that are commonly combined in pipelines for quick log and data analysis?

options.text: awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq, and xargs
hadoop, hive, pig, and oozie
postgres, mysql, sqlite, and redis
gcc, make, ld, and gdb

questions.explanation: awk extracts and transforms fields, sed edits streams, grep filters lines, sort orders lines (spilling to disk if needed), uniq collapses adjacent duplicates, and xargs turns input lines into command arguments. Each does one small job on a text stream, and combining them through pipes covers surprisingly many analyses in a few minutes, with surprisingly good performance. The other groups are a Hadoop stack, database servers, and build and debugging tools.

questions.question: A shell pipeline counts the most popular URLs in a web server log using awk '{print $7}'. An equivalent Ruby program instead reads line.split[6]. What does the Ruby version maintain, and why does the index differ?

options.text: A hash table of counters keyed by the URL; Ruby arrays are zero-indexed while awk fields start at one
A sorted array of every URL it has seen; the indices differ because the two tools read different log formats
A database connection opened per line; the indices genuinely point at two different fields of the log
No state at all between lines; the index is arbitrary and either value would have worked equally well

questions.explanation: The Ruby program keeps a hash table from URL to count, incrementing it for every log line before sorting the totals. awk numbers fields from 1, whereas Ruby arrays are zero-indexed, so awk's field 7 is line.split[6] in Ruby.

questions.question: A shell pipeline (awk, sort, uniq -c, sort -r -n, head) and a short Ruby script that counts URLs in a hash table produce the same top-five report from a web server log. Beyond syntax, what difference in execution becomes apparent on a very large log?

options.text: The script keeps a counter per distinct URL in memory; the pipeline sorts repeats together, and sort can spill to disk
Only the syntax differs: both build the same in-memory table, so they behave identically on input of any size
The pipeline must load the entire log file into memory before awk can start, whereas the script streams it line by line
The script spills its hash table to disk automatically, whereas the pipeline fails once the data exceeds memory

questions.explanation: The Ruby program keeps a hash table mapping each URL to a count, so its memory use grows with the number of distinct URLs. The pipeline has no such table: it sorts the list of URLs so repeats are adjacent and lets uniq -c count runs. GNU sort handles larger-than-memory input by sorting chunks, writing them to disk, and merging them, so the pipeline keeps working when the distinct set would not fit in RAM. Which approach is better therefore depends on the size of the job's working set.

questions.question: To count requests per URL, one program keeps an in-memory hash table of counters, while another sorts the list of URLs and counts adjacent duplicates. What mainly decides which approach is better?

options.text: How many distinct URLs there are, relative to available memory
The total number of log lines, regardless of how many are distinct
Which of the two approaches uses the faster hash function
Whether the log file is stored on a local disk or over the network

questions.explanation: The hash table needs one entry per distinct URL plus a counter, so a million requests for a single URL still take only one entry. If all distinct URLs fit in memory, which is often true for small and mid-sized sites (perhaps within 1 GB), the hash table works fine even on a laptop. If the distinct set exceeds memory, sorting wins because it can sort chunks in memory, write them to disk as sorted segments, and merge them with sequential I/O. The total line count affects running time, but not which approach fits.

questions.question: In a job that counts requests per URL with an in-memory hash table, what is the job's working set, and what does it depend on?

options.text: Memory the job needs random access to; here, set by the number of distinct URLs
The total size of the input log; here it grows with every log line that is read
The size of the output file; here it is just the five most requested URLs
The memory used by the operating system's page cache; here it is fixed by the kernel

questions.explanation: The working set is the amount of memory to which a job needs random access. For per-URL counting, each distinct URL needs one hash-table entry with a counter, so a million log entries for the same URL add nothing beyond that one entry. That is why most small to mid-sized websites could fit all distinct URLs and their counters in about 1 GB. Input size governs how much data is scanned, not how much must be held for random access.

questions.question: When a counting job's working set is larger than available memory, why does a sort-based approach have the advantage over an in-memory hash table?

options.text: Sorted chunks are written to disk as segments and merged with sequential I/O
Sorting needs less CPU than hashing, so it finishes faster on any input size
Sorting can be done entirely inside the CPU cache without touching memory or disk
Sorting avoids reading the input file from disk, unlike building a hash table

questions.explanation: This is the same principle as SSTables and LSM-trees: sort what fits in memory, write it out as a sorted segment file, then merge many sorted segments into a larger sorted file. Mergesort has sequential access patterns that perform well on disk, whereas a hash table larger than memory would need random disk access. GNU sort does this automatically, spilling to disk and using multiple CPU cores, so a simple pipeline scales to large datasets and is typically limited by how fast the input can be read from disk.

questions.question: Who first described the idea behind Unix pipes, roughly when, and with what image?

options.text: Doug McIlroy, in 1964, likening programs to garden-hose segments screwed together
Ken Thompson, in 1970, comparing programs to stations on a factory assembly line
Dennis Ritchie, in 1978, comparing programs to cells cooperating in an organism
Eric Raymond, in 1999, comparing programs to interlocking toy building bricks

questions.explanation: Doug McIlroy, the inventor of Unix pipes, wrote in 1964 that there should be ways of connecting programs like a garden hose, screwing in another segment when data needs to be massaged in another way. The plumbing analogy stuck, and connecting programs with pipes became part of the Unix philosophy, which was written down as a set of design principles in 1978.

questions.question: Which statements accurately represent the Unix philosophy published in 1978? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new 'features'

Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program. Don't clutter output with extraneous information, avoid stringently columnar or binary input formats, and don't insist on interactive input
Design and build software, even operating systems, to be tried early, ideally within weeks. Don't hesitate to throw away the clumsy parts and rebuild them
Use unskilled help in preference to building tools, since the detour to build a tool is always wasteful in the end

questions.explanation: The 1978 statement of the Unix philosophy said: make each program do one thing well; expect every program's output to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program, so avoid extraneous output, stringently columnar or binary formats, and interactive input; build software to be tried early and rebuild clumsy parts; and use tools in preference to unskilled help, even if you must detour to build the tools. The option about preferring unskilled help reverses that fourth principle.

optionExplanations.a: Keeping each program focused makes it composable and replaceable; new behavior is built by combining tools rather than accumulating unrelated features in one program.
optionExplanations.b: Stable, uncluttered stream output allows an unknown future program to consume today's result. Interactive-only or rigid private formats would prevent that composition.
optionExplanations.c: Trying software early exposes awkward design while replacement is still affordable. The philosophy favors experimentation and rebuilding clumsy pieces over defending an initial design.
optionExplanations.d: The published principle says to build tools instead of relying on unskilled help when a tool will pay off. Reversing that advice removes the automation and reuse the philosophy promotes.

questions.question: The Unix philosophy is often compared with today's Agile and DevOps movements. Which qualities does it share with them?

options.text: Automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration, and experimentation
Up-front specification, phase sign-offs, and long release cycles
Central design authority, large monolithic programs, strict change control
Interactive prompts at each step and rich binary output formats

questions.explanation: The principles of small focused programs, composable outputs, trying software early, and building tools to automate work amount to automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration, friendliness to experimentation, and breaking large projects into manageable chunks. Those are the same values emphasized by Agile and DevOps, so surprisingly little has changed in four decades. The other options describe waterfall-style processes or practices the philosophy explicitly discourages, such as interactive input and binary formats.

questions.question: Why is GNU sort a good example of a Unix program that does one thing well, and what is its limitation on its own?

options.text: It spills to disk and parallelizes, yet is barely useful without tools like uniq
It is the fastest Unix tool for any task, so it needs no other tools
It is the simplest Unix tool, but it can only sort data that fits in memory
It bundles sorting, counting, and filtering so that no other tools are needed

questions.explanation: GNU sort is arguably a better sorting implementation than most programming languages have in their standard libraries, which typically neither spill to disk nor use multiple threads. Yet sorting alone rarely answers a question; it becomes powerful in combination with other tools, such as uniq for counting adjacent duplicates. That is the Unix idea: focused tools that compose.

questions.question: What is the uniform interface that lets any Unix program's output be connected to any other program's input?

options.text: A file descriptor: an ordered sequence of bytes
A record made of typed fields with a declared schema
A stream of structured objects passed between processes
A pipe, which is a separate abstraction distinct from files

questions.explanation: In Unix the shared interface is the file, or more precisely the file descriptor, which presents an ordered sequence of bytes. Because that is so simple, many different things can use it: actual files, pipes and stdin/stdout connecting processes, device drivers such as /dev/audio, and TCP sockets. A pipe is itself accessed through file descriptors rather than being a separate interface, and typed records or structured objects are exactly what Unix does not impose.

questions.question: By convention, which record separator do awk, sort, uniq, and head share when they treat a byte stream as text records?

options.text: The newline character (ASCII 0x0A)
The tab character (ASCII 0x09)
The ASCII record separator (0x1E)
The comma, as used in CSV files

questions.explanation: Many Unix tools treat their input as a list of records separated by the newline character (\n, 0x0A). The choice is arbitrary; the ASCII record separator 0x1E was designed for this purpose and would arguably have been better. What matters is that the tools all agree, which lets them interoperate. Splitting a record into fields is less standardized: whitespace, tabs, commas, and other separators are all used.

questions.question: What is a weakness of plain ASCII text as the uniform interface between Unix tools?

options.text: Fields have no names, so tools refer to them by position, like $7
Text is too slow to parse for any realistic volume of log data
Text-processing tools cannot handle input files larger than memory
Every tool must first agree on a binary schema before exchanging data

questions.explanation: Because the interface is untyped text, each tool must parse records itself, and conventions vary (whitespace, tabs, CSV, and so on). Extracting a URL with {print $7} works but is not readable; ideally it would be something like {print $request_url}. Structured, schema-based formats such as Avro and Parquet later addressed this on Hadoop. Text processing is not inherently too slow, and tools like sort handle data larger than memory.

questions.question: How common is Unix-style composability among today's software, such as email services, shopping sites, spreadsheets, and databases?

options.text: It is the exception: few programs can be plugged together that smoothly
It is the norm: most modern applications compose as easily as Unix tools
It is universal among databases that share the same data model
It is guaranteed by web APIs, so data never ends up siloed

questions.explanation: Few programs interoperate as smoothly as Unix tools: you cannot easily pipe your email and online shopping history through a custom analysis tool into a spreadsheet and post the result to a wiki. Even databases with the same data model often make it hard to get data out of one and into another. This lack of integration leads to Balkanization of data, where useful information is trapped in separate systems.

questions.question: What are a Unix program's standard input and standard output connected to if the user specifies nothing else?

options.text: stdin comes from the keyboard and stdout goes to the screen
Files on disk by default, and only a pipe can rebind them
Network sockets by default, with files as the exception
A log file managed by the kernel, for both streams

questions.explanation: Without redirection, a process reads stdin from the keyboard and writes stdout to the screen. The shell can instead redirect either to a file, or use a pipe to attach one process's stdout to another's stdin through a small in-memory buffer. That lets the same program take part in many workflows without knowing who produces or consumes its bytes.

questions.question: A Unix program reads stdin and writes stdout without knowing where its input comes from or where its output goes, leaving the shell user to wire it up. Which established design concepts does this resemble?

options.text: Loose coupling, late binding, and inversion of control
Encapsulation, abstraction, and polymorphism
Tight coupling, early binding, and hard-coded configuration
Shared memory, mutual exclusion, and locking

questions.explanation: Separating I/O wiring from program logic is a form of loose coupling (the program depends only on a byte-stream interface), late binding (the actual input and output are decided when the pipeline is run), and inversion of control (the shell, not the program, decides the connections). That separation is what makes it easy to compose small tools into bigger systems. Tight coupling and hard-coded configuration are the opposite, and the object-oriented and concurrency terms describe unrelated concerns.

questions.question: In a Unix log-analysis pipeline, you want to add your own stages that translate user-agent strings into browser identifiers and IP addresses into country codes. What must your programs do to participate?

options.text: Your program must read from stdin and write to stdout
Your program must register with sort and declare its schema
Your program must be written in C and linked against sort
Your program must implement a plugin interface

questions.explanation: A custom stage only needs to read stdin and write stdout in the agreed record format. sort sees the same byte stream whether its neighbor is a built-in tool or custom code, which separates each stage's logic from pipeline wiring.

questions.question: What are the limits of connecting Unix programs only through stdin and stdout? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Programs that need multiple inputs or outputs are possible but tricky
You cannot pipe a program's output directly into a network connection
A program that opens its own files, subprocesses, or network connections wires that I/O itself, limiting shell rewiring
Unix programs cannot read files at all, only data from standard input

questions.explanation: stdin and stdout give a process one input stream and one output stream wired by the shell. Programs needing several inputs or outputs are possible but awkward; a pipe cannot be pointed directly at a network connection, so a helper such as netcat or curl is needed; and once a program opens its own files, sockets, or subprocesses, that wiring lives inside the program and can only be changed through its own options. Programs can certainly read files directly; doing so just reduces the shell's flexibility.

optionExplanations.a: A process naturally has only one standard input and one standard output stream, so several independent inputs or outputs require conventions such as files, descriptors, or helper processes.
optionExplanations.b: A shell pipe connects local process streams, not directly a remote socket. A program such as netcat can bridge the stream, but that helper owns the network connection.
optionExplanations.c: When code opens its own files, subprocesses, or sockets, those endpoints are hidden behind program-specific configuration. The shell can no longer freely rewire the whole dataflow.
optionExplanations.d: Unix programs can read ordinary files directly and can also receive a file through standard input. The limitation concerns composable wiring, not an inability to access files.

questions.question: Why do Unix tools make it easy to see what is going on in a data-processing pipeline? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Inputs stay immutable, so commands can be rerun safely
Any pipeline stage can be inspected through a pager such as less
Intermediate output can be saved so later stages restart independently
A built-in optimizer explains the globally chosen execution plan

questions.explanation: Unix pipelines are easy to debug for three reasons: input files are normally treated as immutable, so commands can be rerun with different options without damaging them; a pipeline can be ended at any stage and piped into less to inspect intermediate output; and a stage's output can be written to a file, so later stages can be restarted without rerunning everything. They have no query optimizer and are blunt tools compared to a relational database, yet these properties make them excellent for experimentation.

optionExplanations.a: Immutable input lets an operator rerun a command without destroying the source, making experiments and debugging reproducible. Mutation would erase the evidence needed to inspect a failure.
optionExplanations.b: Because each stage emits a normal byte stream, a pager can be inserted to inspect exactly what that stage produced. This makes the pipeline observable one boundary at a time.
optionExplanations.c: Saving an intermediate stream creates a restart point and lets later stages be tested independently. It trades storage for easier diagnosis and incremental experimentation.
optionExplanations.d: Classic Unix pipelines have no global cost-based optimizer explaining a chosen plan. Their transparency comes from simple explicit stages, not automated whole-pipeline planning.

questions.question: What is the biggest limitation of Unix tools for large-scale batch processing, which systems like Hadoop address?

options.text: They run only on a single machine
They cannot be scripted or automated
They cannot process data larger than memory
They cannot read input from files on disk

questions.explanation: A Unix pipeline can use multiple cores (GNU sort parallelizes) and can spill to disk, but it runs on one machine, so its scale is bounded by that machine's disks, CPUs, and I/O bandwidth. MapReduce and HDFS carry the same compositional ideas across potentially thousands of machines. Unix tools do handle larger-than-memory data, are easily scripted, and read files directly.

questions.question: MapReduce is often compared to Unix tools. In what respect is it most like them, and how does it differ?

options.text: Like a Unix process it turns inputs into outputs, but across many machines
Like SQL it is declarative, but it uses shell syntax instead of queries
Like a shell it runs commands, but only on one very large machine
Like a stream processor it handles unbounded events, but stores them in files

questions.explanation: A single MapReduce job is comparable to a single Unix process: it takes one or more inputs and produces one or more outputs, normally without modifying its input or causing other side effects. Like Unix tools it is fairly blunt and brute-force but surprisingly effective. The key difference is that it runs across potentially thousands of machines, reading and writing files on a distributed filesystem rather than using stdin and stdout.

questions.question: Like most Unix tools, how does a MapReduce job normally treat its input and the rest of the system?

options.text: It leaves its input unmodified and has no side effects besides its output
It modifies its input in place and appends new results to existing outputs
It may have arbitrary side effects, as long as it does not modify its input
It may update its input, but must not write anywhere else in the system

questions.explanation: A MapReduce job reads its input without modifying it, and its only effect is producing output files, which are written once, sequentially, and not modified afterwards. This lets the framework retry a failed task safely: rerunning it cannot corrupt the input or duplicate an external action. Arbitrary side effects, such as writing to an external database, would break that safety.

questions.question: Where do MapReduce jobs read input and write output, in place of Unix stdin and stdout, and what is that storage called in Hadoop?

options.text: Files on a distributed filesystem; in Hadoop, HDFS
TCP sockets between tasks; in Hadoop this is YARN
Each machine's local disk only; in Hadoop this is ext4
A message queue; in Hadoop this is Kafka

questions.explanation: MapReduce jobs read and write files on a distributed filesystem. In Hadoop that is HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System, an open source reimplementation of the Google File System (GFS). YARN is Hadoop's resource manager and scheduler rather than its storage, and Kafka is a separate log-based message broker.

questions.question: Which storage systems can play the role HDFS plays for batch jobs, namely durable shared storage that jobs read input from and write output to? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Other distributed filesystems, such as GlusterFS and the Quantcast File System
Object stores such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and OpenStack Swift
A single machine's local filesystem, shared by all of the cluster's tasks
A relational database whose read replicas let it reach petabyte scale

questions.explanation: HDFS is one distributed filesystem among several; GlusterFS and QFS fill the same role, and object stores such as S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Swift are similar in many ways. One difference is that HDFS can schedule a task on a machine that stores a copy of its data, whereas object stores usually keep storage and computation separate. A single machine's filesystem is neither shared across a cluster nor fault-tolerant, and a relational database imposes a data model rather than storing arbitrary files.

optionExplanations.a: GlusterFS and QFS spread file data across many machines' disks and serve it over the network, so tasks across a cluster can read partitioned input from them as they would from HDFS.
optionExplanations.b: Object stores provide durable, scalable storage reachable from many workers, so they can hold batch input and output. They usually separate storage from compute, losing HDFS's ability to run a task next to a local replica.
optionExplanations.c: One machine's local filesystem cannot be reached directly by tasks on other machines and is lost if that machine fails, so it cannot serve as the shared storage layer for a cluster.
optionExplanations.d: Read replicas spread query load but each holds a full copy, and a database requires data to fit its model. It is not a byte-oriented store for arbitrary job input and output at petabyte scale.

questions.question: Which architectural principle is HDFS based on, in contrast to NAS and SAN storage?

options.text: Shared-nothing: ordinary machines with their own disks on a normal datacenter network
Shared-disk: a centralized storage appliance reached over networks such as Fibre Channel
Shared-memory: all machines map one large common memory address space
Shared-everything: every node directly attaches to every disk in the cluster

questions.explanation: HDFS needs no special hardware: each machine contributes its local disks and the nodes communicate over a conventional datacenter network, which is the shared-nothing approach. NAS and SAN are shared-disk architectures built around a centralized storage appliance, often with custom hardware and special networks such as Fibre Channel. Avoiding that hardware is a big reason storage on HDFS is cheaper than equivalent capacity on a dedicated appliance.

questions.question: How is HDFS structured?

options.text: A daemon on each machine serves its local file blocks, and a central NameNode tracks which blocks are where
A single storage server with many disks serves all file blocks to the rest of the cluster
Daemons on each machine serve blocks, with no central metadata; blocks are located by broadcast
A NameNode stores all the file data itself, and the other machines only run computation

questions.explanation: Each machine runs a daemon exposing a network service that lets other nodes access the files stored on that machine's disks. A central server called the NameNode keeps track of which file blocks are stored on which machine. Together they form one big filesystem that uses the disk space of all machines running the daemon. The NameNode holds metadata, not file contents.

questions.question: How does HDFS tolerate machine and disk failures?

options.text: Blocks are copied to several machines, or protected with erasure coding
It relies only on RAID across the disks inside each individual machine
It relies on nightly backups to tape and restores lost files from them
It requires every disk to be mirrored by a central SAN appliance

questions.explanation: HDFS replicates file blocks on multiple machines, so one disk or machine can fail without losing data. Replication can mean full copies of the same data, or an erasure-coding scheme such as Reed–Solomon codes, which recovers lost data with lower storage overhead than full replication. The techniques resemble RAID, but RAID protects disks attached to one machine, whereas HDFS replicates over a conventional datacenter network without special hardware.

questions.question: MapReduce's processing pattern can be compared step by step with the Unix pipeline awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -r -n | head -n 5, which finds popular URLs in a web server log. Which correspondences are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Breaking input files into records corresponds to reading the log one line at a time, with newline as the separator
The mapper that extracts a key and value corresponds to awk '{print $7}', emitting the URL as key with an empty value
The framework's sort of key-value pairs by key corresponds to the first sort command
The reducer that iterates over the sorted pairs corresponds to the second sort command, sort -r -n

questions.explanation: One MapReduce job covers four steps: an input format parser breaks files into records (one log line each); the mapper extracts a key and value (the URL, with an empty value); the framework sorts all pairs by key (the first sort); and the reducer iterates over each key's values (uniq -c, which counts adjacent equal URLs). The second sort, which ranks URLs by count, is not the reducer; in MapReduce it would need a second job.

optionExplanations.a: The input reader splits files into records before user mapping code runs. In a line-oriented web log, the newline boundary naturally defines one request record.
optionExplanations.b: The mapper transforms each record into zero or more key-value pairs; extracting the URL makes requests for the same URL share a grouping key.
optionExplanations.c: Sorting by key brings equal URLs together so the reducer can process each key's complete group. This is framework-managed data movement rather than application code.
optionExplanations.d: The reducer counterpart is the counting operation, such as uniq -c, while the second sort ranks the resulting counts. Confusing the ranking sort with reduction misidentifies the stages.

questions.question: Of MapReduce's four steps (split the input into records, map, sort by key, reduce), which does the job author write code for?

options.text: Steps 2 and 4: the mapper and the reducer
All four steps, including the sort
Only the sort; the framework supplies mapper and reducer
The framework generates all four steps from a declarative query

questions.explanation: The job's developer implements the mapper and reducer callbacks. Splitting files into records is handled by an input format parser, and the sort is implicit: the framework always sorts mapper output before giving it to the reducer. Later dataflow engines make sorting optional, performing it only where an operator needs it.

questions.question: In MapReduce, how is the mapper callback invoked on its input?

options.text: Once per input record, emitting zero or more key-value pairs
It is called once per file and maintains state across records
It must generate exactly one key-value pair per record
It is called once per key and receives all matching records

questions.explanation: The mapper handles each input record independently and may emit any number of key-value pairs, including none. Keeping no hidden state between records allows the framework to split, reorder, and retry map tasks safely.

questions.question: How does the MapReduce framework invoke a reducer?

options.text: Once per key, with an iterator over all of that key's values
Once per key-value pair, with no grouping of values by key
Once per key, after loading all of that key's values into an in-memory list
Once per job, with the whole dataset for the reducer to group itself

questions.explanation: The framework takes the key-value pairs produced by the mappers, collects the values belonging to the same key, and calls the reducer with that key and an iterator over its values. The iterator scans the values incrementally, so one key's values need not all fit in memory. The reducer can then emit any number of output records, such as the number of occurrences of a URL.

questions.question: A Unix log-analysis pipeline uses a second sort to rank URLs by their request counts. How is a second sorting stage like this done with MapReduce?

options.text: Write a second MapReduce job that takes the first job's output as its input
Call a sort routine inside the first job's reducer over all of its output
Configure the framework to run its shuffle sort twice within the same job
It cannot be done, because a MapReduce workflow may contain only one sort

questions.explanation: Each MapReduce job has exactly one implicit sort, between map and reduce. A further sort therefore needs another job: its mapper puts the first job's output into a form suitable for sorting (for example, with the count as the key), and the framework sorts it again before the second reducer. Viewed this way, the mapper's role is to prepare data for sorting and the reducer's role is to process sorted data.

questions.question: What is the main thing MapReduce adds compared with a pipeline of Unix commands?

options.text: It runs the computation in parallel across many machines, with no parallelism code
It adds a declarative query language that the framework evaluates over the input files
It adds ACID transactions spanning several machines, so partial failures roll back
It adds low-latency responses to interactive queries typed by users at a shell

questions.explanation: Mappers and reducers operate on one record (or one key's group) at a time and do not know where their input comes from or where output goes. That lets the framework handle partitioning, moving data between machines, and retrying failures, so the same simple callbacks run in parallel across a cluster. MapReduce is not declarative, transactional, or interactive.

questions.question: What are MapReduce mappers and reducers usually written as?

options.text: Ordinary-language functions, e.g. Java classes in Hadoop
Standard Unix command-line tools, invoked once per record
SQL statements that the framework compiles into tasks
C++ functions, because the framework itself is in C++

questions.explanation: It is possible to use standard Unix tools as mappers and reducers, but they are more commonly functions in a conventional programming language: in Hadoop MapReduce each is a Java class implementing a particular interface, and in MongoDB and CouchDB they are JavaScript functions. The framework handles distributing the code and invoking it on each record or key.

questions.question: In Hadoop MapReduce, what determines how many map tasks a job has, and where does the scheduler try to run them?

options.text: One per input file or block, ideally run on a machine holding a replica of it
A number the job author chooses, with the tasks placed on randomly chosen machines
One map task per machine in the cluster, with the input copied to every machine
One map task per input record, placed on a machine chosen by hashing the record

questions.explanation: A job's input is typically an HDFS directory, and each file or file block is a separate partition processed by its own map task. Input files are often hundreds of megabytes, so the scheduler tries to run each mapper on a machine storing a replica of its input, if that machine has spare RAM and CPU. This is putting the computation near the data: the framework copies the application code (such as JAR files) to that machine instead of moving the large input over the network.

questions.question: In Hadoop MapReduce, how are the number of reduce tasks and the routing of each key to a reducer determined?

options.text: The job author configures the reducer count, and a hash of the key picks each pair's reducer
The reducer count equals the number of input blocks, and the key's first letter picks the reducer
The reducer count equals the number of mappers, and pairs go to reducers in round-robin order
The reducer count is one per machine, and pairs go to whichever reducer is least loaded

questions.explanation: The number of map tasks follows the number of input file blocks, but the number of reduce tasks is configured by the job author and can differ. To ensure that all key-value pairs with the same key reach the same reducer, the framework uses a hash of the key to choose the reduce task. Round-robin or load-based routing would scatter one key's values across several reducers.

questions.question: Before mapper output reaches the reducers, how does Hadoop MapReduce sort it, given that the dataset is too large to sort on one machine?

options.text: Each mapper partitions output by reducer and writes each partition as a sorted local file
All mapper output is written to HDFS and then sorted globally by a single coordinating machine
Mapper output is kept in memory until the end of the job and then sorted in a single pass
Mappers write unsorted output, and every reducer sorts the complete dataset by itself

questions.explanation: Sorting happens in stages. Each map task partitions its output by reducer, based on a hash of the key, and writes each partition to a sorted file on its own local disk, using a technique similar to SSTables. Reducers later fetch their partition from every mapper and merge these sorted files. No single machine ever needs to sort the whole dataset.

questions.question: In MapReduce, what is the shuffle, and why is the name misleading?

options.text: Partitioning mapper output by reducer, sorting it, and copying it to the reducers; nothing about it is random
Randomly reassigning keys among reducers to balance their load; the name describes it accurately
Only the merge-sort performed on the reducer side after fetching; the name describes it accurately
The reduce phase itself, in which values are grouped by key; the name refers to that regrouping

questions.explanation: The shuffle is the process of partitioning map output by reducer, sorting it, and copying each partition from the mappers to the reducer responsible for it. Unlike shuffling a deck of cards, it involves no randomness: a hash of the key deterministically chooses the reducer, so all pairs with the same key meet in one place.

questions.question: When a MapReduce reducer has fetched the sorted partition files for its keys from every mapper, how does it make all records for each key adjacent?

options.text: It merges the already-sorted files, preserving their sort order
It concatenates the files and re-sorts the combined data from scratch
It loads every record into an in-memory hash table keyed by key
It asks each mapper for one key at a time over the network

questions.explanation: Each mapper has already written its output for this reducer as a sorted file, so the reduce task only needs to merge those sorted files, as in the merge step of mergesort. Records with the same key from different mappers end up adjacent in the merged input. The reducer is then called per key with an iterator over those records, and its output is written to the distributed filesystem (typically one copy on the local disk plus replicas on other machines).

questions.question: Why are MapReduce jobs often chained into workflows, and how does Hadoop MapReduce connect one job to the next?

options.text: Each job sorts only once, so multi-stage work needs several jobs, linked by directory name
Each job may read only one input file, so jobs are chained through a built-in workflow API
Each job is limited to a single machine, so jobs are linked through in-memory Unix pipes
Jobs cannot read each other's output, so each one must re-read the original raw input

questions.explanation: A single job can count page views per URL but cannot also rank the URLs, because ranking needs another round of sorting. Hadoop MapReduce has no particular support for workflows: the first job writes its output to a designated HDFS directory, and the second job is configured to read that directory as input. Chained jobs are therefore like commands that each write a temporary file for the next to read, rather than Unix pipes with a small in-memory buffer.

questions.question: When is the output of a batch job in a MapReduce workflow considered valid, and what ensures that downstream jobs wait for it?

options.text: Only once the job succeeds; a workflow scheduler then starts dependent jobs
As soon as any partial output appears; downstream jobs may start immediately
When the first reducer finishes; MapReduce itself then starts the dependent jobs
After a fixed timeout; HDFS file locks block downstream readers until then

questions.explanation: MapReduce discards the partial output of a failed job, so a job's output counts only once it has completed successfully. A job in a workflow can therefore start only after the jobs producing its input directories have finished. Hadoop MapReduce does not track these dependencies itself; workflow schedulers such as Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, Airflow, and Pinball do, and they also help manage large collections of jobs.

questions.question: Roughly how many MapReduce jobs might a workflow for building a recommendation system contain?

options.text: Around 50 to 100 jobs
Rarely more than 2 or 3 jobs
Exactly one job per input dataset
Tens of thousands of jobs, one per user

questions.explanation: Workflows of 50 to 100 MapReduce jobs are common when building recommendation systems, and in a large organization many teams run jobs that read each other's output. At that size, coordinating dependencies by hand is impractical, which is why workflow schedulers and higher-level tools (Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch, FlumeJava) that wire multi-stage workflows together automatically matter. By comparison, Google's original search-index build was a workflow of 5 to 10 jobs.

questions.question: When is a join needed, and does denormalization eliminate that need?

options.text: When code needs both sides of a reference; denormalization only reduces this
Only in relational models; document and graph models embed data and never need joins
Only after denormalizing; fully normalized data never requires joins
Only for graph edges; denormalization removes every other kind of join

questions.explanation: Records often reference other records: a foreign key in the relational model, a document reference in the document model, or an edge in a graph model. A join is needed whenever code must access both the record holding the reference and the record being referenced. Denormalization copies some referenced data into the referencing record, which reduces the need for joins but generally does not remove it entirely. It is normalization, not denormalization, that creates the need for joins.

questions.question: MapReduce has no indexes in the usual sense. How does a MapReduce job access its input, and when is that reasonable?

options.text: It scans every input file in full, which suits jobs aggregating many records
It builds a fresh index for each job on the fly and then performs indexed lookups
It uses HDFS's built-in indexes, which are faster than scans for every kind of query
It reads only the records a query needs, by seeking directly to their byte offsets

questions.explanation: Given a set of files as input, a MapReduce job reads their entire content, which a database would call a full table scan. That is outrageously expensive for retrieving a few records, where an index lookup is far better. But analytic workloads often aggregate over a large number of records, and scanning everything in parallel across many machines is then reasonable. Batch joins likewise resolve an association for all records at once, rather than looking up the data for one user.

questions.question: An analytics job joins a log of logged-in users' actions on a website with a database of user profiles. In star-schema terms, what is the activity log commonly called, and what role does it play?

options.text: Clickstream data, serving as the fact table, with user profiles as a dimension
A dimension table, with the user database acting as the fact table that holds the events
A snapshot table, which is joined to the user database by matching timestamps
A denormalized table that already embeds every user's full profile in each event

questions.explanation: The log of things logged-in users did on a website is called activity events or clickstream data. In a star schema it is the fact table (many events, each carrying a user ID), and the user database is one of the dimensions. The events contain only the user ID, not the profile, because embedding the profile in every event would be wasteful; that is why a join is needed, for example to find which pages are most popular with which age groups.

questions.question: A batch job joins a huge log of activity events with user profiles by querying a remote user database once per event. Why would this likely perform poorly? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The processing throughput would be limited by the round-trip time to the database server
The effectiveness of a local cache would depend very much on the distribution of data
Running a large number of queries in parallel could easily overwhelm the database
Each query would scan the whole user table, since databases cannot look up records by key

questions.explanation: Each event would wait for a network round trip, so throughput is limited by the round-trip time to the database; a local cache helps only if the distribution of user IDs gives good hit rates; and many parallel tasks issuing queries could easily overwhelm the database. The general rule is that good batch throughput requires the computation to be local to one machine as much as possible. Querying a live database would also make the job nondeterministic, because the data might change while it runs. Each query is an indexed point lookup, not a table scan; the problem is the per-event round trip and the aggregate load.

optionExplanations.a: A synchronous remote lookup adds at least one network round trip per event, putting database latency directly on the critical path and severely limiting batch throughput.
optionExplanations.b: A cache helps only when accesses have enough locality and the working set fits. Uniformly distributed user IDs can produce a low hit rate and preserve most remote lookups.
optionExplanations.c: Thousands of batch tasks can issue queries concurrently and overload connection pools, CPU, or I/O on the operational database. The batch job then harms both itself and production traffic.
optionExplanations.d: A database finds a user by primary key through an index, so each query is a cheap point lookup rather than a table scan. The cost lies in the network round trip per event and the combined load of many such queries.

questions.question: For a batch join between a large activity log and a user-profile database, what is preferable to looking up each event's user in the live database?

options.text: Copy the user database, e.g. from a backup, into the same distributed filesystem as the log
Query the live database from the reducers instead of from the mappers, to reduce load
Copy the whole activity log into the user database and run the join there instead
Have every mapper fetch each profile from the live database and cache it locally

questions.explanation: Taking a copy of the user database (for example, extracted from a backup using an ETL process) and putting it in HDFS alongside the activity logs means both inputs are just files. MapReduce can then bring the related records together and process them with sequential, local I/O, avoiding per-record network requests. Because the copy does not change during the job, the result is also deterministic. Querying from reducers, or caching per mapper, still depends on the live database.

questions.question: In a reduce-side sort-merge join of activity events with user profiles, what key and value do the two sets of mappers emit?

options.text: Both key by user ID; activity mappers emit the event, profile mappers the birth date
Both use the event timestamp as key, so that records are joined in time order
Only activity mappers emit pairs; profiles are loaded into each reducer's memory
Both use the date of birth as key, so that users of the same age meet at one reducer

questions.explanation: The join key is the user ID. One set of mappers reads the activity events and emits the user ID as key with the activity event as value; another reads the user database and emits the user ID as key with the user's date of birth as value. Partitioning and sorting by key then bring each user's profile record and all of that user's events to the same reducer, so the join needs no network lookups.

questions.question: In a reduce-side sort-merge join, which technique ensures that the reducer receives the user-profile record before that user's activity events?

options.text: Secondary sort, so the database record arrives first
Primary sort, which orders by key only
Total order partitioning, which orders reducers
Combiner ordering, which pre-aggregates on the map side

questions.explanation: A secondary sort orders the records within each key: here, the reducer for a user ID sees the user-database record first, followed by that user's activity events in timestamp order. The reducer can store the date of birth in a local variable and then stream through the events. Sorting by key alone guarantees grouping but not the order within a group; total-order partitioning and combiners address different concerns.

questions.question: In a reduce-side sort-merge join that uses a secondary sort, how is the reducer called, and how much user data must it hold in memory?

options.text: Once per user ID; it holds only that user's profile while iterating over the events
Once per activity event; it queries the user database separately for each event
Once for the whole job; it buffers every user's records in memory at the same time
Once per user ID; it must buffer all of that user's events before it sees the profile

questions.explanation: The reducer is called once for every user ID. Thanks to the secondary sort, the first value is the user's date-of-birth record, which the reducer stores in a local variable; it then iterates over that user's activity events, emitting pairs such as viewed URL and viewer age. It never holds more than one user record at a time and never makes a network request. Subsequent jobs could then compute, for example, the distribution of viewer ages for each URL.

questions.question: MapReduce is sometimes described as mappers sending messages to reducers. What plays the role of the destination address?

options.text: The key: all pairs with the same key are delivered to the same reducer call
An IP address and port number that the mapper writes into each record
A TCP connection that each mapper opens directly to a reducer it picks
The input file name, which tells the reducer where the data came from

questions.explanation: When a mapper emits a key-value pair, the key acts like a destination address for the value. It is an arbitrary string rather than a network address, but it behaves like one: every pair with the same key is delivered to the same destination, a single call to the reducer. The framework handles the actual network transfer.

questions.question: What does the MapReduce programming model separate, and what benefit for failure handling follows?

options.text: Networking from application logic, so failed tasks can be retried transparently
Reads from writes; written data becomes durable without needing any replication
Storage from compute; clusters can grow and shrink elastically on demand
Mappers from reducers; jobs gain nothing beyond a tidier organization of the code

questions.explanation: MapReduce separates the physical network communication (getting data to the right machine) from the application logic (processing the data once it is there). In typical database use, by contrast, requests to fetch data occur deep inside application code. Because the framework handles all network communication, it also shields application code from partial failures such as another node crashing, transparently retrying failed tasks.

questions.question: Besides joins, what other common operation uses MapReduce's pattern of bringing all records with the same key to the same place?

options.text: Grouping records by key and aggregating each group, as with SQL's GROUP BY
Filtering out the records that fail a condition, before writing output
Projecting each record down to a few of its fields to shrink the output
Parsing raw text lines into structured records with typed fields

questions.explanation: Grouping, as in SQL's GROUP BY, uses the same shuffle as joins: mappers emit the grouping key, partitioning sends equal keys to one reducer, and sorting makes the group's records adjacent. The reducer can then count records (COUNT(*)), sum a field (SUM), or pick the top k by some ranking. Filtering, projection, and parsing act on one record at a time, so they need no co-location.

questions.question: In batch analysis of website activity logs, what is sessionization, and how is it implemented with MapReduce?

options.text: Collating one user session's events, grouped by session cookie or user ID
Splitting each user's events across many reducers to balance the processing load
Counting the total number of page views per day across all users of the site
Removing duplicate events that happen to share the same timestamp and user ID

questions.explanation: Sessionization collects all activity events for a particular user session to find the sequence of actions the user took, for example to see whether users shown a new site version (an A/B test) are more likely to buy. With many web servers, one user's events are scattered across different servers' log files. Using a session cookie or user ID as the grouping key brings them together at one reducer, while different users' events are spread across partitions.

questions.question: When does MapReduce's pattern of sending all records with the same key to one reducer break down?

options.text: When one key, like a celebrity's user ID, has a disproportionate amount of data
When there are many more distinct keys than there are reducers in the job
When the input files have not been sorted before the mappers start reading them
When the records for one key arrive at the reducer from several different mappers

questions.explanation: A hot key, also called a linchpin object (for example a celebrity with millions of followers), sends a huge number of records to one reducer, causing skew or a hot spot. Because a job is complete only when all its tasks finish, every downstream job waits for that slowest reducer. Many distinct keys are fine because they spread across reducers, mapper input need not be sorted, and records from many mappers meeting at one reducer is exactly how the shuffle works.

questions.question: How does Pig's skewed join method handle hot keys in a join?

options.text: It samples to find hot keys, then spreads each across several reducers
It routes all hot-key records to one dedicated reducer with more memory
It drops hot-key records and processes them later in a separate pass
It hashes hot keys twice so that they land on two fixed reducers

questions.explanation: Pig's skewed join first runs a sampling job to find which keys are hot. During the join, mappers send records for a hot key to one of several reducers chosen at random, instead of the single reducer the key's hash would pick. Records for that key from the other join input must be replicated to all of those reducers so every match is found. This parallelizes the hot key's work at the cost of duplicating part of the other input.

questions.question: Pig, Crunch, and Hive each have a technique for joins with hot keys. Which description matches them correctly?

options.text: Pig samples to find hot keys; Crunch needs them declared; Hive stores them separately and map-side joins them
All three detect hot keys with a sampling job and then assign their records to reducers at random
All three require hot keys to be declared in table metadata and store those keys' records in separate files
Pig requires hot keys to be declared explicitly, while Crunch and Hive both detect them using a sampling job

questions.explanation: Pig's skewed join runs a sampling job to find hot keys, then spreads them over several reducers while replicating the other input. Crunch's sharded join is similar but requires the hot keys to be specified explicitly. Hive's skewed join optimization also needs hot keys declared, in the table metadata; it stores their records in separate files and uses a map-side join for those keys.

questions.question: When grouping and aggregating records by a hot key in MapReduce, how can the work be split into two stages?

options.text: Stage one sends records to random reducers that each aggregate a subset; stage two combines them
A single stage configured with many more reducers than usual, so the hot key is split automatically
A first stage that drops the hot key's records and a second stage that reprocesses only those records
Two stages that each aggregate the full dataset independently, whose results are then compared

questions.explanation: The first MapReduce stage sends the hot key's records to random reducers, so each reducer groups only a subset and outputs a more compact aggregated value per key (for example a partial count). A second job then combines the values from all first-stage reducers into a single value per key. Simply adding reducers to one stage does not help, because all of one key's records still go to one reducer.

questions.question: Why are sort-merge joins in MapReduce called reduce-side joins, and what are their main advantage and cost?

options.text: Join logic runs in reducers; any input layout works, but sorting, copying, and merging are costly
The join logic runs in the mappers; they are fast, but require both inputs to be sorted in advance
The reducers do the sorting; they need no assumptions about the input and add no extra cost
HDFS performs the join itself; the only cost is the extra network load on the storage nodes

questions.explanation: In a reduce-side join the mappers only prepare the data (extracting keys and values, assigning pairs to reducer partitions, and sorting), while the actual join logic runs in the reducers. The advantage is that no assumptions about the input are needed: whatever its structure, the mappers can prepare it. The cost is that sorting, copying to reducers, and merging reducer inputs can be expensive, and data may be written to disk several times along the way.

questions.question: Which kind of MapReduce join uses a cut-down job with no reducers and no sorting, and is possible only when the inputs satisfy certain assumptions?

options.text: A map-side join
A reduce-side sort-merge join
A skewed join with sampling
A two-stage grouped aggregation

questions.explanation: If you can make assumptions about the input, such as one side being small or both sides being partitioned the same way, a map-side join is possible. Each mapper reads one input file block from the distributed filesystem and writes one output file; there is no reducer and no sort. A reduce-side join is the opposite trade-off: it needs no assumptions but pays for the shuffle.

questions.question: In a broadcast hash join, what condition must the inputs meet, and what do the words broadcast and hash refer to?

options.text: One input is small enough to fit in memory; every mapper loads all of it into a hash table
Both inputs are small; the joined result is broadcast to every reducer by hash
The small input is hash-partitioned; each mapper loads only its own hash bucket
The large input fits in memory; it is broadcast to each mapper of the small input

questions.explanation: A broadcast hash join applies when a large dataset is joined with one small enough to load entirely into memory in each mapper. Each mapper of the large input first reads the whole small input into an in-memory hash table, then scans its block of the large input and looks up each record's key. Broadcast reflects that every partition of the large input receives the entire small input; hash reflects the use of a hash table. Pig calls this a replicated join and Hive a MapJoin.

questions.question: In a broadcast hash join, what alternative to an in-memory hash table can hold the small join input, and why is it nearly as fast?

options.text: A read-only index on local disk, whose hot parts stay in the OS page cache
A remote database that is queried once for each record of the large input
A file in HDFS that each mapper rereads from the start for every input record
A hash table spread across all of the mappers and accessed over the network

questions.explanation: Instead of loading the small input into memory, it can be stored in a read-only index on local disk. The frequently used parts of that index remain in the operating system's page cache, so lookups are almost as fast as an in-memory hash table, but the dataset no longer has to fit entirely in memory. Remote or network-distributed lookups would reintroduce per-record network latency.

questions.question: A map-side partitioned hash join combines activity events with user profiles; both inputs are split into 10 partitions by the last decimal digit of the user ID. What does mapper 3 do, and why is that sufficient?

options.text: It loads users whose ID ends in 3 into a hash table and scans their events; matches share partition 3
It loads the whole user database, as a broadcast join would, and scans partition 3 of the events
It reads all ten partitions of both inputs, so that matches in any partition are found
It loads events whose user ID ends in 3 and queries the live database for each user

questions.explanation: Because both inputs are partitioned identically, all records that could join are in the same-numbered partition. Mapper 3 loads all users with an ID ending in 3 into a hash table, then scans all activity events for users whose ID ends in 3. Each mapper reads only one partition of each input, so its hash table holds about a tenth of the user data instead of all of it.

questions.question: What must be true of both inputs for a map-side partitioned hash join to work, and what does Hive call this join?

options.text: Same partition count, key, and hash function; Hive calls it a bucketed map join
Either input may be partitioned in any way; Hive calls it a MapJoin
Both must be sorted by the key but need not be partitioned; Hive calls it a merge join
Any layout works once the inputs are compressed; Hive calls it a skewed join

questions.explanation: Records can be joined within matching partitions only if both inputs have the same number of partitions, with records assigned using the same key and the same hash function. If the inputs were produced by earlier MapReduce jobs that already grouped data this way, that is a reasonable assumption. Hive calls partitioned hash joins bucketed map joins; its MapJoin is the broadcast hash join.

questions.question: What additional property of the inputs makes a map-side merge join possible, and why does memory size then not matter?

options.text: Both are partitioned and sorted alike by the key, so a mapper merges them incrementally
Both are small enough to fit in memory, so a mapper loads each one into its own hash table
Both are unsorted, so the mapper can sort them in memory before matching records
Both are stored in the same file, so the mapper needs to read only one file
