questions.explanation: If the inputs are not only partitioned the same way but also sorted by the same key, a mapper can do what a reducer normally does: read both files incrementally in ascending key order and match records with equal keys. No hash table is needed, so the inputs need not fit in memory. Such inputs were probably produced by earlier jobs; the join could have been done there, but a separate map-only job makes sense if the sorted datasets are also needed for other purposes.

questions.question: When a join's output feeds downstream jobs, how does the choice between a reduce-side and a map-side join affect the output's layout?

options.text: Reduce-side output is partitioned and sorted by join key; map-side output follows the large input's layout
Both kinds of join produce output that is partitioned and sorted by the join key
Map-side output is grouped by join key, while reduce-side output keeps the large input's file-block layout
Neither kind of join produces partitioned output, so downstream jobs must always reshuffle

questions.explanation: A reduce-side join's output is partitioned and sorted by the join key, because that is how data reached the reducers. A map-side join starts one map task per file block of the large input, whether it is a broadcast or a partitioned join, so its output is partitioned and sorted like that large input. Because map-side joins depend on such physical layout, metadata about partition counts and keys (kept, for example, in HCatalog and the Hive metastore) matters when optimizing joins.

questions.question: How do OLTP queries and analytic queries typically differ, and where does batch processing fit?

options.text: OLTP fetches a few records by key, analytics scans many; batch scans similarly but often outputs datasets
OLTP scans whole tables, analytics fetches records by key; batch processing is a form of OLTP
Both fetch a few records by key; batch processing is identical to analytics in every respect
Both scan whole tables; batch processing differs only in always producing human-readable reports

questions.explanation: OLTP queries generally look up a small number of records by key using indexes, to present them to a user. Analytic queries scan many records, performing groupings and aggregations, and their output is often a report for an analyst or manager. Batch processing is closer to analytics because it scans large portions of its input, but its output is often not a report; it may be a search index, a key-value database, or another dataset.

questions.question: What was Google's original use of MapReduce, and roughly how large was that workflow?

options.text: Building its search indexes, as a workflow of 5 to 10 jobs
Crawling the web, as a workflow of 50 to 100 MapReduce jobs
Computing PageRank scores for every page, in a single job
Serving live search queries, with one MapReduce job per query

questions.explanation: Google first used MapReduce to build the indexes for its search engine, implemented as a workflow of 5 to 10 MapReduce jobs. Google later moved away from MapReduce for this purpose, but index building remains a useful lens for understanding it, and Hadoop MapReduce remains a good way to build Lucene/Solr indexes. Serving live queries is online processing, not batch, and workflows of 50 to 100 jobs are typical of recommendation systems.

questions.question: Why is batch processing well suited to building a document-partitioned full-text search index over a fixed set of documents?

options.text: Mappers partition the documents; each reducer builds an immutable index for its partition
Mappers build the index and reducers answer search queries against it, updating it in place
A single reducer builds one global index for all documents, which is then updated in place
Indexes are built only at query time, so the batch job never needs to write output files

questions.explanation: For full-text search over a fixed set of documents, the mappers partition the documents as needed, each reducer builds the index (term dictionary and postings lists) for its partition, and the index files are written to the distributed filesystem. Document-partitioned indexes parallelize very well because each partition is built independently. Since querying a search index by keyword is read-only, the index files are immutable once created.

questions.question: When the set of documents covered by a batch-built search index changes, what are the two ways to update the index?

options.text: Rerun the whole build and swap files, or write new segments merged in the background
Only incremental updates are possible, because rebuilding would lose the old documents
Only full rebuilds are possible, because immutable index files cannot gain new segments
Edit the existing index files in place, locking them while queries are paused

questions.explanation: The simplest option is to periodically rerun the entire indexing workflow and replace the previous index files wholesale. That is computationally expensive if only a few documents changed, but very easy to reason about: documents in, indexes out. Alternatively, indexes can be built incrementally, as Lucene does: it writes new segment files and asynchronously merges and compacts them in the background, without modifying existing segments.

questions.question: Besides search indexes, which kinds of systems are commonly built with batch jobs, and what form does their output often take?

options.text: Classifiers and recommendation systems, often output as a key-value database
Business reports, since batch output is read by analysts rather than applications
Online transaction systems, whose output is a stream of new user requests
More search indexes, since batch output must take the form of postings lists

questions.explanation: Batch processing is widely used to build machine learning systems such as classifiers (spam filters, anomaly detection, image recognition) and recommendation systems (people you may know, related products). Their output is often a database that the web application queries, for example by user ID to get suggested friends or by product ID to get related products. That raises the question of how batch output reaches a database the application can query.

questions.question: A batch job's mappers or reducers could write their results straight into a production database one record at a time. Why is that a bad idea? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One network request per record destroys batch throughput
Many parallel tasks can overwhelm the destination database
External writes expose partial and speculative task effects
Databases accept only one writer, so parallel clients are rejected

questions.explanation: A network request per record is orders of magnitude slower than a batch task's normal throughput, even with client-side batching. Many tasks writing concurrently at batch rates can overwhelm the database and degrade its query performance for other parts of the system. And writing to an external system breaks MapReduce's all-or-nothing output guarantee: results of partially completed jobs, retried task attempts, and speculative execution become visible to others. Databases do accept many concurrent writers; the problems are load and correctness, not a single-writer rule.

optionExplanations.a: A remote write for every record replaces sequential local processing with network latency and protocol overhead. This defeats the high-throughput access pattern batch systems depend on.
optionExplanations.b: Many mapper and reducer instances run in parallel, so their combined write load can saturate the destination's connections, indexes, locks, or storage bandwidth.
optionExplanations.c: Tasks may be retried or speculatively duplicated, exposing partial output and duplicate writes outside the framework's atomic file publication. External side effects are not automatically rolled back.
optionExplanations.d: Most databases accept multiple writers and coordinate them with transactions or concurrency control. The risk is overload and duplicated effects, not an inherent single-writer restriction.

questions.question: What output guarantee does MapReduce normally provide for a job, even when some tasks fail and are retried?

options.text: On success, output is as if each task ran exactly once; on failure, there is no output
Partial output is visible while the job runs and is cleaned up afterwards only if the job fails
Every task attempt's output is kept, including the output of failed and retried attempts
Only reducer output is all-or-nothing; output of failed map tasks is kept and reused

questions.explanation: MapReduce gives a clean all-or-nothing guarantee: when a job succeeds, the result is the output of running every task exactly once, even if some tasks failed and were retried along the way; if the job fails, no output is produced. Output from failed or duplicate (speculative) task attempts is discarded. This works only because tasks have no externally visible side effects, which is why writing to an external database from inside a job breaks it.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to get a batch job's results into a key-value database that serves read-only queries?

options.text: Build new database files inside the job, write them to the distributed filesystem, then bulk-load them
Have each reducer write its records directly into the production database in small batches
Export the results to CSV files and have an operator import them into the database manually
Have each mapper send its records through a message queue that writes them to the database

questions.explanation: Rather than writing into a live database, the job builds a brand-new database as files in its output directory, just like a search index. These immutable files are then loaded in bulk into servers that handle read-only queries; Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB, and HBase bulk loading support this. Extracting keys and sorting by them is most of the work of building such an index, and read-only files need no write-ahead log. Voldemort, for instance, keeps serving the old files while copying the new ones, atomically switches over, and can switch back if something goes wrong.

questions.question: MapReduce follows the Unix discipline of treating inputs as immutable and replacing output without other side effects. Which benefits follow from that discipline? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Buggy output can be fixed by reverting the code and rerunning, or by switching back to the old output
Failed tasks can be rerun automatically on the same input, because failed output is discarded
Easy rollback lets feature development move faster than where mistakes cause irreversible damage
Retried tasks can reuse the partial output left behind by a failed attempt to save work

questions.explanation: Because inputs are never modified and outputs simply replace earlier output, a bad deployment can be undone by rolling back the code and rerunning the job, or by switching back to old output kept in another directory; this human fault tolerance is something read-write databases lack. Minimizing irreversibility in this way speeds up development. The framework can retry failed tasks safely precisely because inputs are immutable and the output of failed tasks is discarded; reusing partial output would defeat that.

optionExplanations.a: Since the input is unchanged and the output is derived, rerunning fixed code reproduces correct output, and older output kept in a separate directory allows an instant switch back. A database that buggy code has overwritten cannot be repaired by rolling back the code.
optionExplanations.b: A rerun reads the same immutable input, and the failed attempt's output has been discarded, so the retry cannot see half-written data. Transient faults are tolerated automatically, while genuine code bugs eventually fail the job.
optionExplanations.c: When mistakes are cheap to undo, teams can deploy and experiment more freely. Minimizing irreversibility is a principle that benefits agile software development.
optionExplanations.d: The framework deliberately discards output from failed tasks because it may be incomplete. Reusing it would let a retry build on uncertain partial results and break the all-or-nothing output guarantee.

questions.question: Unix tools pass untyped text, so each tool must parse its input. What do Hadoop jobs gain by using structured file formats such as Avro and Parquet instead?

options.text: They avoid repeated text parsing and support compatible schema evolution
They make records human-readable, so jobs can be debugged with less and grep
They give the same parsing cost as text, since both pass untyped records
They remove the need for any agreed interface between consecutive jobs

questions.explanation: Plain-text pipelines repeatedly interpret delimiters and fields at each stage. Avro and Parquet carry a schema and use efficient structured encodings, reducing parsing overhead while allowing compatible schema changes over time. Both are binary encodings, so they are not meant to be read as plain text.

questions.question: In what sense was the 2004 MapReduce paper not at all new?

options.text: Its parallel processing and join algorithms existed in MPP databases a decade earlier
MapReduce was copied from Hadoop, which had been released several years before it
MapReduce had already been fully described in the 1978 statement of the Unix philosophy
It merely repackaged Pregel's vertex-centric graph-processing model for general data

questions.explanation: Massively parallel processing (MPP) databases such as the Gamma database machine, Teradata, and Tandem NonStop SQL had implemented the same parallel processing and join algorithms more than a decade earlier. The biggest difference is purpose: MPP databases focus on parallel execution of analytic SQL queries, while MapReduce plus a distributed filesystem behaves more like a general-purpose operating system that can run arbitrary programs. Hadoop is an implementation of MapReduce, not its predecessor.

questions.question: What do databases (including MPP databases) require of data that a distributed filesystem such as HDFS does not, and what does that enable?

options.text: A data model chosen up front; HDFS holds any bytes, so raw data can be dumped first
Sorted input; HDFS accepts unsorted data, so jobs reading from it never need to sort
Immutable data; HDFS allows any job to edit files in place, so data can be corrected later
Compressed input; HDFS stores data uncompressed, so jobs can skip decoding it later

questions.explanation: Databases require data to fit a particular model (relational, document, and so on), and MPP databases typically need careful up-front modeling of data and query patterns before import into their proprietary storage format. Files in a distributed filesystem are just byte sequences in any encoding: text, images, sensor readings, feature vectors, genome sequences. Hadoop thus made it possible to dump data into HDFS first and only later figure out how to process it; in practice, making data available quickly is often more valuable than designing the ideal model up front.

questions.question: Which named ideas describe raw-first data collection? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data lake or enterprise data hub: collect raw data from across the organization first, design schemas later
Schema-on-read: the consumer, not the producer, interprets the data when reading it
The sushi principle: raw data is better
Schema-on-write: design one complete schema before any data is loaded

questions.explanation: Collecting raw data first and modeling it later goes by several names. A data lake or enterprise data hub brings data from across an organization together quickly, enabling joins across previously separate datasets. Schema-on-read shifts interpretation from the producer to each consumer, which helps when they are different teams with different priorities. The sushi principle (raw data is better) notes that raw data supports many different derived views. Schema-on-write, designing one model before loading, is the opposite approach typical of MPP databases.

optionExplanations.a: A data lake or enterprise hub collects disparate raw datasets before forcing one warehouse schema, enabling later cross-source joins. It prioritizes acquisition speed and future reuse.
optionExplanations.b: Schema-on-read lets each consumer interpret stored bytes for its own purpose when it reads them. The flexibility shifts validation and modeling work from ingestion to consumption.
optionExplanations.c: The sushi principle is the mnemonic that minimally processed source data preserves more possible future uses. It does not mean corrupt or undocumented data is automatically valuable.
optionExplanations.d: Designing one complete schema before loading is schema-on-write, the careful up-front modeling MPP databases typically require. It is the opposite of raw-first collection.

questions.question: How is Hadoop commonly used for ETL alongside an MPP data warehouse?

options.text: Raw OLTP dumps go to HDFS; MapReduce jobs clean and reshape them for the warehouse
Hadoop replaces the warehouse entirely, so no transformation is ever performed
The warehouse cleans the raw data itself, and Hadoop only archives the final results
OLTP systems transform their own data before writing it into the warehouse

questions.explanation: Data from transaction processing systems is dumped into the distributed filesystem in some raw form; MapReduce jobs then clean it up, transform it into a relational form, and import it into an MPP data warehouse for analytics. Data modeling still happens, but as a separate step decoupled from data collection. That decoupling is possible because a distributed filesystem accepts data encoded in any format.

questions.question: MPP databases are monolithic, tightly integrated systems handling storage layout, query planning, scheduling, and execution. What does that integration buy them?

options.text: Very good performance on its target queries, plus SQL usable from analyst tools
The flexibility to run arbitrary user code, at the cost of slower SQL queries
Cheap fault tolerance through retrying individual failed tasks of a query
The ability to store data in any format at all, without up-front modeling

questions.explanation: Because the storage layout, planner, scheduler, and executor can all be tuned for the database's specific needs, an MPP database achieves very good performance on the types of queries it was designed for. SQL also allows expressive queries without writing code, making it accessible to graphical tools used by business analysts, such as Tableau. The price is flexibility: arbitrary code and arbitrary data formats are what Hadoop-style systems offer instead, and MPP databases usually abort a whole query when a node fails.

questions.question: Machine learning, recommendation systems, relevance-ranked search indexes, and image analysis are often run as batch jobs. Why do they need a processing model more general than SQL?

options.text: They need application-specific code, such as feature engineering, not expressible as SQL
Only reporting workloads need general code; these workloads fit naturally into SQL queries
SQL can already express all of these workloads fully, without any extensions at all
These workloads need specialized hardware rather than a different programming model

questions.explanation: Processing such as feature engineering for machine learning, natural language models for translation, or risk estimation for fraud prediction is very specific to the application, so it inevitably requires writing code, not just queries. MapReduce gave engineers the ability to run their own code over large datasets. A SQL engine can be built on top of it (as Hive did), but many batch processes do not lend themselves to being expressed as SQL.

questions.question: Hadoop supported both SQL-style processing (for example via Hive) and MapReduce. Why were further processing models later built on Hadoop?

options.text: MapReduce proved too limited and slow for some work, and Hadoop's openness allowed others
Hive's SQL proved slower than raw MapReduce, so a model between the two was needed
HDFS could store only files written by MapReduce, so new storage formats were needed
MPP databases already offered every model, so Hadoop had to copy each of them in turn

questions.explanation: People found MapReduce too limiting and too slow for some kinds of processing, so other models were developed on top of Hadoop. Because the platform is open, a whole range of approaches could be implemented, which would not have been possible within a monolithic MPP database. Crucially, they can all run on one shared cluster over the same files in HDFS. Hive's SQL engine was itself built on top of MapReduce, so the problem was MapReduce's own limits, not a gap between SQL and MapReduce.

questions.question: What is the advantage of running several processing models (MapReduce, an analytic engine like Impala, a database like HBase) on one shared Hadoop cluster?

options.text: They all access the same HDFS files, so data need not be imported into separate specialized systems
Each model gets its own isolated storage, so the models can never interfere with each other
Only MapReduce-based tools can run there, so behaviour is uniform across the whole cluster
The cluster runs only one model at a time, so there is never any contention for resources

questions.explanation: In the Hadoop approach, different processing models run on a single shared-use cluster, all reading the same files in the distributed filesystem. There is no need to import data into several specialized systems, which makes it easier to derive value from data and to experiment with new processing models. HBase (a random-access OLTP database) and Impala (an MPP-style analytic engine) do not use MapReduce at all, yet both store data in HDFS and coexist in the same system.

questions.question: Besides diversity of storage and of processing models, which two further design differences separate MapReduce from MPP databases?

options.text: How faults are handled, and how memory and disk are used
The choice of query language, and the on-disk storage format
The network topology, and the policy for scheduling queries
The transaction isolation level, and the replication factor

questions.explanation: If a node crashes during a query, most MPP databases abort the whole query and rerun it, which is acceptable because queries usually run for seconds or minutes; they also keep as much data in memory as possible, for example using hash joins. MapReduce instead retries individual failed tasks without affecting the job as a whole, and is very eager to write data to disk, partly for fault tolerance and partly on the assumption that datasets are too big for memory.

questions.question: For what kind of environment was MapReduce originally designed, explaining its task-level recovery and sparing use of memory?

options.text: Mixed-use datacenters in which higher-priority work often preempts batch tasks
Dedicated batch-only clusters with no task priorities and no other workloads running
Clusters of unusually unreliable hardware where machines fail every few minutes
Supercomputers running one job at a time with exclusive use of every node

questions.explanation: At Google, online production services and offline batch jobs run on the same machines. Every task has a resource allocation enforced by containers and a priority; if a higher-priority task needs resources, lower-priority tasks on that machine can be terminated (preempted). This lets non-production resources be overcommitted for better utilization, but low-priority MapReduce tasks risk being killed at any time. Hardware failures, by contrast, are rare enough that most jobs would not experience one.

questions.question: At Google, a MapReduce task running for an hour had about a 5% risk of being preempted. For a job of 100 tasks that each run for 10 minutes, roughly what is the risk that at least one task is terminated before finishing?

options.text: Greater than 50%
About 5%, the same as for one task
About 0.8%, since each task runs a sixth of an hour
Close to 100%, since 100 times 5% exceeds 100%

questions.explanation: Assume preemptions are independent and the hourly risk is spread evenly over time. A ten-minute task survives with probability about 0.95^(1/6), roughly 0.9915. All 100 tasks survive with probability about 0.9915^100, roughly 0.43, so the risk that at least one is killed is about 57%, greater than 50%. Each task's own risk is under 1%, but it compounds across many tasks; multiplying 100 by 5% wrongly ignores both the task length and the overlap between events.

questions.question: Why is MapReduce designed to tolerate frequent unexpected termination of tasks?

options.text: Being free to kill low-priority tasks lets a shared cluster use its resources better
Commodity hardware fails so constantly that most tasks crash at least once during a job
Networks drop so many packets that tasks must be restarted continually to make progress
Disks wear out within hours under batch workloads, killing the tasks running on them

questions.explanation: It is not because hardware is particularly unreliable: Google's preemption rate was more than an order of magnitude higher than its rate of failures from hardware issues and reboots. The design lets a scheduler arbitrarily terminate processes, which enables better resource utilization. Open source schedulers used preemption less: at the time of writing, YARN's CapacityScheduler preempted only to balance queues, and general priority preemption was not supported in YARN, Mesos, or Kubernetes, so in such environments MapReduce's design decisions make less sense.

questions.question: MapReduce is one of many possible programming models for distributed batch processing. In what sense is it simple, and why is it worth studying?

options.text: Simple to understand, though laborious to use; its clear abstraction makes it a good learning tool
Simple to use, and still the fastest option for almost every kind of batch workload
Simple to use and to understand, and the only programming model available on Hadoop
Simple only in its internal implementation, so it offers little worth studying today

questions.explanation: MapReduce is a fairly clear and simple abstraction on top of a distributed filesystem: simple in the sense that you can understand what it is doing, not in the sense of being easy to use. Implementing a complex job with the raw MapReduce APIs is hard and laborious; you would even have to implement join algorithms from scratch. It is worth studying as a learning tool, while other tools may be more appropriate depending on data volume, data structure, and the type of processing.

questions.question: Pig, Hive, Cascading, and Crunch were built as higher-level abstractions on top of MapReduce. What did they improve, and what limitation remained?

options.text: They simplified programming, but MapReduce's execution costs remained
They simplified execution, but mapper and reducer programming stayed unchanged
They removed HDFS materialization, but supported only handwritten callbacks
They added stream processing, but could no longer execute bounded batch jobs

questions.explanation: Pig, Hive, Cascading, and Crunch were created because raw MapReduce is hard to use; their higher-level constructs make many common batch tasks much easier to implement. But some problems lie in the MapReduce execution model itself, such as fully materializing intermediate state and always sorting between stages, and adding another level of abstraction does not fix the resulting poor performance. MapReduce is very robust on unreliable multi-tenant clusters, while other tools can be orders of magnitude faster for some workloads.

questions.question: In a workflow of chained MapReduce jobs, what does materialization of intermediate state mean, and how do Unix pipes differ?

options.text: Writing each job's intermediate output to files in full; pipes stream it through a small buffer
Computing results only on demand when requested; pipes instead write every stage's output to files
Storing intermediate results in a database; pipes instead store them in a distributed filesystem
Caching intermediate results in RAM only; pipes instead write intermediate data to disk first

questions.explanation: When one job's output is used only as another job's input, those files are just intermediate state. Writing that state out to files is called materialization: eagerly computing a result and writing it out, as with materialized views, rather than computing it on demand. Unix pipes do not fully materialize intermediate state; they stream output to the next process's input incrementally through a small in-memory buffer.

questions.question: What are the downsides of MapReduce fully materializing intermediate state between the jobs of a workflow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Stages cannot overlap, and stragglers delay the entire workflow
Redundant mappers often reread freshly materialized reducer output
Temporary intermediate files receive unnecessary distributed replication
Materialized files cannot be reread after a failure

questions.explanation: Fully materializing intermediate state has three downsides. A job can start only when every task of the preceding jobs has finished, so a few straggler tasks (caused by skew or uneven load) delay the whole workflow. Mappers are often redundant, just reading back a file that a reducer has just written and preparing it for the next partition and sort. And intermediate files in a distributed filesystem are replicated across several nodes, which is overkill for temporary data. The durability of materialized files is actually an advantage for fault tolerance, not a downside.

optionExplanations.a: A downstream MapReduce job cannot start until the upstream job has fully materialized output, so stages cannot pipeline and one straggler holds up the whole workflow.
optionExplanations.b: Every materialized boundary is read again by a new set of mappers, even when the data was just produced. That repeated serialization and disk I/O adds no application value.
optionExplanations.c: HDFS normally replicates intermediate files for durability although many are temporary and cheaply recomputable. Network transfer and storage are spent on data that soon disappears.
optionExplanations.d: Materialization makes intermediate files durable and therefore easy to reread after failure. The downside is excessive I/O and waiting, not loss of recoverability.

questions.question: Which are the best-known dataflow engines developed to fix MapReduce's problems with materialized intermediate state?

options.text: Spark, Tez, and Flink
Hive, Pig, and Cascading
HBase, Impala, and Drill
Oozie, Azkaban, and Airflow

questions.explanation: Spark, Tez, and Flink handle an entire workflow as one job rather than breaking it into independent subjobs, and they explicitly model the flow of data through several processing stages, hence the name dataflow engines. Hive, Pig, and Cascading are higher-level languages that can run on top of such engines; HBase and Impala are databases and query engines on HDFS; Oozie, Azkaban, and Airflow are workflow schedulers.

questions.question: Dataflow engines connect operators (their generalized processing functions) in several ways. Which descriptions of these connection options are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Send the same output of one operator to all partitions of a join operator, for broadcast hash joins
Repartition and sort records by key, as in MapReduce's shuffle, for sort-merge joins and grouping
Repartition several inputs the same way without sorting, saving effort for partitioned hash joins
Send a broadcast input to just one partition of the join operator, chosen by hashing the key

questions.explanation: Unlike in MapReduce, operators in a dataflow engine need not alternate strictly between map and reduce. One operator's output can be repartitioned and sorted by key (enabling sort-merge joins and grouping), repartitioned without sorting (enough for partitioned hash joins, since building a hash table discards order anyway), or broadcast to every partition of a downstream join. Broadcasting to only one partition would leave the others without the small input.

optionExplanations.a: Broadcast sends the same complete output to every partition of the downstream join operator, so each partition of the large input can probe a full hash table of the small input.
optionExplanations.b: Repartitioning and sorting by key reproduces MapReduce's shuffle, grouping equal keys in sorted order, which is what sort-merge joins and grouping need.
optionExplanations.c: Partitioned hash joins need matching keys to land in the same partition but not in any order, because building a hash table discards the order anyway, so skipping the sort saves work.
optionExplanations.d: Sending the small input to only one hashed partition would leave the other partitions of the large input without the lookup data they need, so matches would be missed.

questions.question: Which advantages do dataflow engines have over chained MapReduce jobs? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sort and repartition only where a graph edge requires them
Use whole-graph visibility to improve task and data locality
Keep temporary state in memory or local disk instead of replicated HDFS
Wait for an entire upstream stage before starting downstream work

questions.explanation: Dataflow engines sort only where an operator actually requires it, eliminate redundant map tasks by folding them into the preceding operator, let the scheduler make locality optimizations because all joins and data dependencies are declared, keep intermediate state in memory or on local disk instead of replicated HDFS, start operators as soon as their input is ready, and reuse JVM processes. Waiting for a whole upstream stage to finish is MapReduce's behaviour. As a result, the same computations usually run significantly faster, and Pig, Hive, or Cascading workflows can switch from MapReduce to Tez or Spark by a configuration change.

optionExplanations.a: A general dataflow graph can leave records in place unless a particular edge needs partitioning or sorting. MapReduce imposes a shuffle boundary for every reduce stage.
optionExplanations.b: Seeing the full operator graph lets the scheduler co-locate dependent work, reuse partitions, and choose better execution order. Separate MapReduce jobs hide those opportunities.
optionExplanations.c: Temporary data can stay in memory or local disk and be regenerated from lineage after failure. It need not be written and replicated through HDFS at every stage.
optionExplanations.d: Waiting for all upstream tasks is the MapReduce materialization barrier. Dataflow operators can normally begin as partitions of their inputs become available.

questions.question: How does Tez differ from Spark and Flink in what it provides?

options.text: Tez is a thin library using YARN's shuffle service; Spark and Flink bring their own runtime
Tez is a large framework with its own runtime; Spark and Flink are thin libraries over YARN
All three are thin libraries that rely on YARN's shuffle service to transfer data
All three include their own network layer, scheduler, and high-level user APIs

questions.explanation: Tez is a fairly thin library that relies on the YARN shuffle service for the actual copying of data between nodes. Spark and Flink are big frameworks that include their own network communication layer, scheduler, and user-facing APIs. Because dataflow operators generalize map and reduce, workflows written in Pig, Hive, or Cascading can switch from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with a configuration change, while Spark and Flink also offer their own high-level dataflow APIs.

questions.question: Dataflow engines avoid writing intermediate state to HDFS. How do they recover when a machine fails and its intermediate state is lost?

options.text: They recompute it from data still available, tracking lineage (Spark) or checkpointing state (Flink)
They replicate all intermediate state synchronously to three machines, exactly as HDFS does
They always restart the entire job from the beginning, rereading all of the original input
They require operators to write their state to an external database after every record

questions.explanation: MapReduce makes recovery easy by writing intermediate state durably to HDFS. Spark, Flink, and Tez avoid that, so if a machine fails and its intermediate state is lost, they recompute it from data that is still available: an earlier intermediate stage if possible, otherwise the original input on HDFS. To do so the framework tracks how each piece of data was computed. Spark's resilient distributed dataset (RDD) abstraction records the ancestry of data, while Flink checkpoints operator state so it can resume an operator that hit a fault.

questions.question: Dataflow engines recover lost data by recomputing it. Why does it matter that operators are deterministic, and which are common sources of nondeterminism? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recomputed data must match what downstream operators already received, or they must be rerun too
Iterating over a hash table, whose order many programming languages do not guarantee
Probabilistic or statistical algorithms that use random numbers without a fixed seed
Reading the system clock, which returns the same value on every execution

questions.explanation: If lost data is recomputed after some of the original was already sent downstream, the new data must match; otherwise downstream operators face contradictions and normally must be killed and rerun, causing cascading recomputation. Nondeterminism creeps in easily: hash-table iteration order is often unspecified, probabilistic algorithms use random numbers, and the system clock or external data sources give different answers on each run. Generating pseudorandom numbers from a fixed seed is one way to remove it. Recomputation is not always best: if intermediate data is much smaller than its source, or very CPU-intensive to compute, materializing it is cheaper.

optionExplanations.a: Lineage-based recovery is safe only if recomputation reproduces data that downstream operators may already have consumed. Different output could make one logical run internally inconsistent.
optionExplanations.b: Hash-table traversal order may depend on memory layout or runtime details, so the same records can be emitted in a different sequence. Order-sensitive downstream code can then diverge.
optionExplanations.c: Randomized algorithms need controlled seeds or recorded choices to reproduce output. Fresh randomness during recovery can generate a result inconsistent with the original attempt.
optionExplanations.d: System clocks differ across machines and advance between attempts, making clock reads a classic source of nondeterminism. Treating them as identical would invalidate recomputation assumptions.

questions.question: In terms of the Unix analogy, how do MapReduce and dataflow engines differ, and which kind of operator cannot be fully pipelined?

options.text: MapReduce is like temp files, dataflow engines like pipes; sorting needs all its input first
Dataflow engines resemble temp files and MapReduce resembles pipes; a filter must see all input first
Both pipe data between every stage like Unix; a join must always see all of its input first
Both write every stage to temporary files; no operator ever needs to see all of its input first

questions.explanation: MapReduce is like writing each command's output to a temporary file, whereas dataflow engines look much more like Unix pipes; Flink in particular is built around pipelined execution, passing output incrementally to the next operator. Sorting is the exception: it must consume its entire input before producing output, because the last input record could have the lowest key. A job's initial input and final output still usually live as materialized files in HDFS; the saving is in not materializing the intermediate state.

questions.question: How does whole-graph batch processing differ from OLTP-style graph traversal queries, and what does PageRank compute?

options.text: Batch jobs run algorithms over the whole graph rather than OLTP-style traversals; PageRank ranks a page by what links to it
Batch jobs look up single vertices quickly while OLTP traversals analyse whole graphs; PageRank ranks pages by their size
They are the same use case at two different scales; PageRank simply counts the edges leaving each vertex in the graph
Both walk a few edges out from a chosen starting vertex; PageRank ranks users by how much activity they generate

questions.explanation: OLTP-style graph queries quickly find a small number of vertices matching some criteria by following a few edges. In a batch context the goal is offline analysis of the entire graph, often for recommendation engines or ranking systems. PageRank, one of the most famous such algorithms, estimates a web page's popularity from which other pages link to it, and is part of how web search engines order their results.

questions.question: Dataflow engines and graph processing both involve graphs. Why is conflating the two a mistake?

options.text: A dataflow engine's graph is a DAG of operators, whereas graph processing analyses graph-structured data
They really are the same thing: a dataflow DAG is just one way of drawing a graph algorithm out
Graph processing needs a cyclic operator graph, which no dataflow engine is able to express at all
Dataflow DAGs cannot express iterative algorithms, so graph algorithms must fall back on MapReduce

questions.explanation: Dataflow engines such as Spark, Flink, and Tez arrange a job's operators as a directed acyclic graph (DAG): the graph describes how data flows between operators, while the data itself is usually relational-style tuples. In graph processing, the data itself is a graph of vertices and edges. The shared word graph is an unfortunate naming coincidence; dataflow engines can still run iterative graph algorithms, for example through Pregel-style APIs such as Spark's GraphX and Flink's Gelly.

questions.question: How are many graph algorithms, such as transitive closure, expressed?

options.text: Follow one edge at a time, propagating information, and repeat until a condition holds
In a single pass over all edges, after which the result is final without repetition
By sorting all vertices by degree and then processing each exactly once in that order
By a single SQL join between the vertex table and the edge table, run only once

questions.explanation: Many graph algorithms traverse one edge at a time, joining a vertex with an adjacent vertex to propagate some information, and repeat until a condition is met, such as no more edges to follow or some metric converging. Transitive closure is a case in point: finding all locations contained within North America by repeatedly following edges that say which location is within which other location. A single pass or a single join reaches only immediate neighbors.

questions.question: Why does plain MapReduce fit iterative graph algorithms poorly, even though they can be run step by step with an external scheduler?

options.text: Each job is one pass that rereads the whole input and rewrites all output, even if little changed
MapReduce cannot store graphs at all, because HDFS rejects files made of vertex and edge lists
Each job keeps the whole graph in memory between iterations, which exhausts RAM on large graphs
MapReduce supports iteration natively, but only for graphs small enough to fit in one machine's memory

questions.explanation: The idea of repeating until done cannot be expressed in plain MapReduce, which performs a single pass over the data. So an external scheduler runs a batch process for one step, checks the completion condition (for example, no more edges to follow, or change below a threshold), and runs another round if needed. This works but is often very inefficient: each iteration reads the entire input dataset and produces a completely new output, even if only a small part of the graph changed since the last iteration. MapReduce keeps no state between jobs, so nothing is held in memory from one iteration to the next.

questions.question: Which graph-processing model lets vertices retain state across synchronized rounds?

options.text: Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP), also known as the Pregel model
The MapReduce iteration model, run by an external workflow scheduler
Stateless dataflow operators chained into one long DAG
The actor model, in which actors exchange messages asynchronously

questions.explanation: The bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) model, popularized by Google's Pregel paper and implemented by Apache Giraph, Spark's GraphX, and Flink's Gelly, runs in iterations. In each one, a function is called for every vertex with the messages sent to it; the vertex remembers its state in memory between iterations, so it only processes new messages, and parts of the graph receiving no messages need no work. Actors also keep state but lack synchronized rounds and framework-provided durability.

questions.question: In the Pregel model of graph processing, how do vertices communicate, and what is the parallel with MapReduce?

options.text: By sending messages along edges, much as mappers send values to reducers by key
By reading neighboring vertices' state directly from shared memory, with no messages
By writing results to HDFS for other vertices to read in a later MapReduce job
By querying a central coordinator that stores the state of every vertex in the graph

questions.explanation: In MapReduce, mappers conceptually send a message to a particular reducer call, because the framework collects all outputs with the same key. Pregel works similarly: one vertex sends a message to another vertex, typically along an edge. In each iteration, a function is called for each vertex with all the messages sent to it, much like a reducer call; unlike MapReduce, the vertex keeps its state between iterations. Vertices never query each other directly.

questions.question: Pregel resembles the actor model if each vertex is seen as an actor. How does it differ from typical actors? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Vertex state and messages between vertices are fault-tolerant and durable
Communication proceeds in fixed rounds: messages sent in one iteration are all delivered in the next
Pregel vertices cannot send messages at all, unlike actors
Pregel vertices carry no state between iterations, unlike actors

questions.explanation: Two differences stand out. Pregel makes vertex state and messages fault-tolerant and durable, whereas actors normally leave that to the application. And communication proceeds in fixed rounds: at every iteration the framework delivers all messages sent in the previous one, a timing guarantee actors normally lack. Pregel implementations also guarantee that each message is processed exactly once at its destination vertex in the following iteration, even if the underlying network drops, duplicates, or delays messages.

optionExplanations.a: Pregel checkpoints vertex state and provides reliable delivery semantics across worker failure. Ordinary actor systems often leave durability and message guarantees to the application.
optionExplanations.b: Pregel advances through global supersteps: messages sent in one round become inputs in the next. Actors generally process asynchronously without a framework-wide round boundary.
optionExplanations.c: Pregel vertices communicate by sending messages along graph edges or to vertex IDs. The model restricts direct shared-state access, not messaging itself.
optionExplanations.d: A vertex retains mutable state across supersteps, which is central to iterative graph algorithms. Calling it stateless confuses Pregel with stateless MapReduce callbacks.

questions.question: How does a Pregel-style system recover when a node fails and its in-memory vertex state is lost?

options.text: It rolls back to the last checkpoint of all vertex state, taken at the end of an iteration, and restarts
It keeps synchronous replicas of every vertex on three machines and fails over to one of them
It reruns the whole computation from the original input, because it never takes checkpoints
It skips the lost vertices and carries on, because graph algorithm results are approximate anyway

questions.explanation: Pregel periodically checkpoints the state of all vertices at the end of an iteration, writing their full state to durable storage. If a node fails and its in-memory state is lost, the simplest recovery is to roll back the entire graph computation to the last checkpoint and restart. If the algorithm is deterministic and messages are logged, it is also possible to selectively recover only the partition that was lost.

questions.question: In Pregel, what does a vertex need to know about where other vertices run, and how is the graph usually partitioned in practice?

options.text: Only vertex IDs; the framework places vertices, often by arbitrarily assigned ID
Each target's machine; the graph is partitioned to keep neighbors together
Only vertex IDs; the framework always finds an optimal partitioning that colocates neighbors
Each target's machine; vertices are moved to random machines at every iteration

questions.explanation: A vertex simply sends messages to a vertex ID; the framework decides which machine runs each vertex and routes messages over the network (thinking like a vertex). Ideally, vertices that communicate a lot would be colocated, but finding such a partitioning is hard, so in practice the graph is often partitioned by an arbitrarily assigned vertex ID, with no attempt to group related vertices. That leads to a lot of cross-machine communication.

questions.question: Distributed graph processing often suffers heavy cross-machine message traffic. When is a distributed framework such as Pregel actually necessary?

options.text: Only when the graph is too big for one machine; otherwise one machine is often faster
Whenever the graph has more than a few million edges, since one machine cannot keep up
Whenever the graph exceeds one machine's memory, even if it fits on that machine's disks
Only when the graph is small enough to fit entirely in one machine's memory

questions.explanation: Because graphs are often partitioned arbitrarily, distributed graph algorithms send many messages between machines, and the intermediate state can be bigger than the original graph. So if a graph fits in memory on one computer, a single-machine (even single-threaded) algorithm will quite likely outperform a distributed batch job. If it exceeds memory but fits on one machine's disks, a single-machine framework such as GraphChi is viable. Only when the graph is too big for one machine is a distributed approach like Pregel unavoidable.

questions.question: As distributed batch infrastructure matured to store and process many petabytes on clusters of over 10,000 machines, where did attention turn?

options.text: Running at scale was considered solved; focus moved to programming models and efficiency
Scale became the only remaining problem, so focus moved to building ever larger clusters
Batch processing was abandoned, because stream processing had replaced it entirely
Focus moved from software to hardware, building custom shared-disk storage appliances

questions.explanation: Once the infrastructure became robust enough to store and process many petabytes of data on clusters of over 10,000 machines, the problem of physically operating batch processes at that scale was considered more or less solved. Attention turned to improving the programming model, improving the efficiency of processing, and broadening the set of problems these technologies can solve, for example through high-level APIs, declarative query optimizers, and domain-specific libraries.

questions.question: Why did higher-level languages and APIs such as Hive, Pig, Cascading, and Crunch become popular, and what extra benefit did they gain when Tez appeared?

options.text: Raw MapReduce is laborious; their jobs could move to Tez without code rewrites
They ran faster than MapReduce, but every job had to be rewritten to run on Tez
They supported stream processing from the start, which Tez required of its users
They removed the need for a cluster, which Tez then made entirely unnecessary

questions.explanation: Programming MapReduce jobs by hand is quite laborious, so higher-level languages and APIs became popular. When Tez emerged, they gained the additional benefit of moving to the new dataflow execution engine without rewriting job code, because their relational-style operators describe what to compute rather than how to wire map and reduce stages. Spark and Flink provide their own high-level dataflow APIs, often inspired by FlumeJava.

questions.question: Beyond requiring less code, what advantage do high-level dataflow APIs bring to batch processing development?

options.text: Interactive, incremental development in a shell
They eliminate the need for a cluster
They guarantee exactly-once external side effects
They give low-latency responses to end users

questions.explanation: Besides needing less code, high-level interfaces allow interactive use: writing analysis code incrementally in a shell and running it frequently to observe what it does. That is very helpful for exploring a dataset and experimenting with processing approaches, and it is reminiscent of the Unix philosophy. These interfaces also improve job execution efficiency at the machine level, because the framework can optimize the declared operations.

questions.question: When joins are specified as relational operators rather than hand-written code, what can a cost-based optimizer in Hive, Spark, or Flink do?

options.text: Choose a join algorithm from the inputs' properties and reorder joins to cut intermediate state
Rewrite user-defined callback functions into faster machine code by analyzing what they compute
Choose only the number of reducers to allocate, leaving the join algorithm to the user
Guarantee that every join runs as a broadcast hash join, the fastest algorithm in all cases

questions.explanation: If the application simply states which joins are required, the framework can analyze properties of the join inputs and automatically decide whether a sort-merge, broadcast hash, or partitioned hash join fits best, and even change the order of joins to minimize intermediate state. The choice of join algorithm can make a big difference to performance, and declarative specification spares users from understanding all the algorithms. A user-defined function's code is opaque, so it cannot be rewritten this way, and no single join algorithm is fastest for all inputs.

questions.question: How do MapReduce and its dataflow successors differ from SQL's fully declarative query model, and what advantage does that bring?

options.text: They run user callbacks that may call arbitrary code, so existing libraries apply
They are fully declarative too, so no user-written code ever runs inside a job
They use a restricted expression language without callbacks, so they always run faster
They differ only in syntax, so exactly the same optimizations always apply to both

questions.explanation: MapReduce was built around function callbacks: for each record or group of records, a user-defined function (the mapper or reducer) is called and is free to run arbitrary code. That lets jobs draw on large ecosystems of existing libraries for parsing, natural language analysis, image analysis, and numerical or statistical algorithms. Databases do support user-defined functions, but they are often cumbersome to use and poorly integrated with package managers such as Maven, npm, and Rubygems.

questions.question: Why do dataflow engines benefit from expressing even simple filters and field selections declaratively instead of as callback functions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Calling a callback for every record costs significant CPU even for a trivial filter
Declared filters and projections let the optimizer read only the needed columns from columnar storage
Engines such as Hive, Spark DataFrames, and Impala can use vectorized execution in tight, cache-friendly loops
These engines deliberately avoid code generation, since interpreting callbacks directly is faster

questions.explanation: If a callback only checks a simple condition or selects some fields, calling it on every record wastes significant CPU. Expressed declaratively, the same operations let the optimizer exploit column-oriented storage and read only the required columns, and let engines use vectorized execution: tight inner loops friendly to CPU caches, with no per-record function calls. These engines also generate code: Spark emits JVM bytecode and Impala uses LLVM for native code. With these features batch frameworks start to match MPP databases in performance while keeping the ability to run arbitrary code.

optionExplanations.a: Every opaque function call adds per-record overhead, so wrapping a trivial predicate or projection in a callback costs CPU without adding any capability.
optionExplanations.b: A declarative list of required fields lets the optimizer read only those columns from columnar storage. Opaque callback code hides that information and forces broader reads.
optionExplanations.c: Vectorized execution processes batches in tight cache-friendly loops rather than crossing a function boundary for every row. This improves CPU efficiency for simple operators.
optionExplanations.d: Spark and Impala can generate JVM bytecode or native code for hot loops. Claiming code generation is deliberately avoided reverses an important optimization.

questions.question: Batch frameworks can run arbitrary code. Why are reusable implementations of common algorithms still valuable, and which are examples?

options.text: Standard patterns recur; examples are Mahout, MADlib, and k-nearest neighbors
Arbitrary code already suffices, so libraries exist only for business reporting
Reusable libraries exist only inside MPP databases, never on batch engines
Reusable algorithms are needed only because user callbacks cannot call libraries

questions.explanation: While running arbitrary code is useful, standard processing patterns keep recurring, so reusable implementations of common building blocks pay off. Mahout implements machine learning algorithms on top of MapReduce, Spark, and Flink, while MADlib implements similar functionality inside a relational MPP database (Apache HAWQ). Spatial algorithms such as k-nearest neighbors support similarity search, and approximate string matching serves genome analysis. As batch engines gain such features and MPP databases become more programmable, the two look increasingly alike.

questions.question: Which design principles of Unix tools carried forward into MapReduce and later dataflow engines?

options.text: Immutable inputs, outputs that feed other programs, and composing small tools
Monolithic programs, typed interactive input, and updating data files in place
Careful up-front data modeling, with every record validated as it is written
Outputs updated in place by later jobs, so results are never replaced wholesale

questions.explanation: Inputs are immutable, outputs are intended to become the input to another (as yet unknown) program, and complex problems are solved by composing small tools that each do one thing well. In Unix the composition interface is files and pipes; in MapReduce it is a distributed filesystem, and dataflow engines add their own pipe-like transport for intermediate data.

questions.question: What is the uniform interface that lets programs be composed in Unix, in MapReduce, and in dataflow engines?

options.text: Unix: files and pipes; MapReduce: a distributed filesystem; dataflow: that plus pipe-like links
Unix: pipes only; MapReduce: in-memory pipes between jobs; dataflow engines: only replicated files
All three: a shared relational database that every processing stage reads and writes
Unix: network sockets; MapReduce: a message queue; dataflow engines: shared memory

questions.explanation: In Unix, the uniform interface that lets one program be composed with another is files and pipes. In MapReduce it is the distributed filesystem: each job reads input directories and writes output directories. Dataflow engines add their own pipe-like data transport to avoid materializing intermediate state to the distributed filesystem, but a job's initial input and final output usually still live in HDFS.

questions.question: What are the two main problems that distributed batch processing frameworks need to solve?

options.text: Partitioning, to bring related data together, and fault tolerance
Replication and compression of the input files stored in HDFS
Scheduling and monitoring of multi-job workflows across teams
Encoding and serialization of individual records between tasks

questions.explanation: Partitioning: MapReduce partitions mappers by input file blocks, then repartitions, sorts, and merges mapper output into reducer partitions so that all records with the same key end up together; dataflow engines avoid sorting unless required but partition in a broadly similar way. Fault tolerance: MapReduce writes to disk frequently, so an individual failed task can be recovered without restarting the job, at the cost of slower failure-free execution; dataflow engines keep more in memory and must recompute more after a failure, which deterministic operators make easier.

questions.question: Which descriptions of join algorithms used by MapReduce (and also by MPP databases and dataflow engines) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sort-merge: mappers extract the join key, and partitioning and sorting bring matching records to one reducer call
Broadcast hash: a small input is loaded into a hash table in every mapper of the large input
Partitioned hash: inputs partitioned identically are hash-joined partition by partition
Broadcast hash: both inputs are partitioned and sorted, then merged by each reducer

questions.explanation: In a sort-merge join, each input passes through mappers that extract the join key, and partitioning, sorting, and merging bring all records with the same key to the same reducer call, which outputs the joined records. In a broadcast hash join, one input is small enough to load entirely into a hash table in each mapper, which then scans its partition of the large input. In a partitioned hash join, both inputs use the same key, hash function, and number of partitions, so the hash approach is applied to each partition independently. Partitioning, sorting, and merging belong to sort-merge joins, not to broadcast hash joins.

optionExplanations.a: Mappers emit the join key, and the shuffle's partitioning and sorting make every record for a key adjacent at one reducer call, which combines both sides. This works for any input layout at the cost of sorting and copying.
optionExplanations.b: Because the small input fits in memory, each mapper of the large input loads all of it into a hash table and looks up each large-input record locally, with no reducers or shuffle.
optionExplanations.c: When both inputs share the key, hash function, and partition count, matching records sit in same-numbered partitions, so each mapper builds a hash table from only its partition of one input.
optionExplanations.d: A broadcast hash join avoids partitioning and sorting altogether by copying the whole small input to each mapper. Partitioning, sorting, and merging describe the sort-merge join instead.

questions.question: Distributed batch frameworks restrict what mapper and reducer callbacks may do. Which restriction lets the framework retry tasks safely and discard failed output?

options.text: Callbacks must be stateless and have no externally visible side effects
Callbacks may be stateful and have side effects, which the framework tracks
Callbacks must finish within a fixed time limit set by the scheduler
Callbacks must be written in SQL so that the framework can analyze them

questions.explanation: Callbacks are assumed to be stateless and to have no externally visible side effects besides their designated output. That lets the framework hide hard distributed-systems problems: after crashes or network issues, tasks can be retried safely, output from failed tasks is discarded, and if several attempts for a partition succeed, only one becomes visible. The final output is then the same as if no faults had occurred, much stronger semantics than online services that write to databases as a side effect of handling requests.

questions.question: What is the distinguishing feature of a batch processing job, and what property of its input lets it finish?

options.text: It derives output without modifying input, and bounded input lets it finish
It gives the lowest possible latency per record, and its input never ends
It keeps input and output in HDFS, and the input is updated in place as it runs
It always has one map and one reduce step, and its input is an endless stream

questions.explanation: A batch job reads some input data and produces output without modifying the input, so the output is derived from the input. Crucially, the input is bounded: it has a known, fixed size, such as a set of log files at some point in time or a snapshot of a database. Because of that, the job knows when it has finished reading the entire input and eventually completes. Stream processing, by contrast, has unbounded input, so its jobs never complete.
